Look at the bottoms: 2, 4, 7, 14 and 28. Which one do all the others go into?

ask.ifNot: 4 does not go into 14. But 2, 4, 7 and 14 all go into 28, so twenty-eighths will work for everything.

beats.say: So we turn everything into twenty-eighths. The whole 1 is 28 over 28. One half is 14 over 28, and one quarter is 7 over 28.
1 over 7 is 4 over 28, and 1 over 14 is 2 over 28. The last one, 1 over 28, stays as it is.
Now every piece is the same size, so we just add the tops. 28, 14, 7, 4, 2 and 1 make 56.
So the total is 56 over 28. What is that as a whole number?

ask.ifNot: 56 over 28 means 56 divided by 28. 28 and 28 make 56, so 28 goes in exactly 2 times.

beats.say: 56 divided by 28 is 2. So the whole sum is exactly 2.
Isn't that neat? All those little fractions fill up exactly one more whole. The plan: pick the bottom number everything fits into, change each fraction, then add the tops.
We need the H C F of three numbers: the biggest number that divides 54, 288 and 360 exactly.
54 first. It is even, so 2 comes out. What is left splits into 3 times 3 times 3.
288: halve it five times and 9 is left, which is 3 times 3.
And 360 is 2 times 2 times 2, times 3 times 3, times 5.
The H C F uses only primes that all three numbers have. How many 2s do all three share?

ask.ifNot: 54 has only one 2. So however many the others have, only one 2 is shared by all three.

beats.say: One 2 is shared. And the 3s? 54 has three of them, but 288 and 360 have only two each. So two 3s are shared.
The 5 belongs only to 360, so it stays out. Multiply what is shared: 2 times 3 times 3 is 18. So the H C F is 18.
Check: 54 divided by 18 is 3, 288 divided by 18 is 16, and 360 divided by 18 is 20. All exact.
Notice that 54 itself cannot be the H C F, because 54 does not go into 288. With three numbers, a prime only counts if every number has it.
After selling 15 dozen bananas, a man gains 45 rupees. How many dozen must he sell to gain 84 rupees?
Good news first. The question talks in dozens and asks for dozens. So we never need to count single bananas at all.
What should we find first?

ask.ifNot: Find one first. If we know the gain on 1 dozen, we can count how many dozens bring in 84 rupees.

beats.say: 45 rupees from 15 dozen. 45 divided by 15 is 3. So each dozen gains him 3 rupees.
He wants a gain of 84 rupees, at 3 rupees a dozen. What do we do?

ask.ifNot: Every dozen brings in 3 rupees. So we count how many times 3 goes into 84, and that is a division.

beats.say: 84 divided by 3 is 28.
He should sell 28 dozen bananas.
Check: 28 dozen at 3 rupees each. 28 times 3 is 84. And a bigger gain needed more dozens than 15, which makes sense.
So find the gain on one, then count how many ones you need. And only change the units when the question makes you.
Here is our equation. 4 a, minus 5, equals 2 a, plus 3. This time the letter is on both sides.
We want all the a terms on one side. Which move does that?

ask.ifNot: The 2 a on the right is a plus 2 a. To undo it we take 2 a away, and we take it from both sides so the balance stays level.

beats.say: So we take 2 a from both sides. On the right it is gone. On the left, 4 a take away 2 a leaves 2 a.
Now it is one we know well. What is in the way of the 2 a?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side. The 2 a has a minus 5 hanging on to it. That goes next.

beats.say: To undo minus 5 we add 5, to both sides. 3 plus 5 is 8, so 2 a equals 8.
2 a means 2 times a, so we divide both sides by 2. 8 divided by 2 is 4. So a equals 4.
Check both sides with a as 4. Left: 4 times 4, minus 5, is 11. Right: 2 times 4, plus 3, is 11. Both sides are 11, so it balances.
When the letter is on both sides: gather the letters on one side, then the numbers on the other, then divide.
Something divides 91 a b c and gives 7 c. We have to find that something.
Try the idea with small numbers. 12 divided by 4 is 3. And if we did not know the 4, we could find it: 12 divided by 3 is 4.
So to find a missing divider, we divide the big one by the answer. Our missing piece is 91 a b c divided by 7 c.
Numbers first. What is 91 divided by 7?

ask.ifNot: Try 7 times 13. 7 times 10, and 7 times 3, added together make 91. So 91 divided by 7 is 13.

beats.say: 91 divided by 7 is 13.
Now the letters: a b c divided by c. What is left?

ask.ifNot: There is a c on top and a c underneath. c divided by c is 1, so the c cancels. Only a b is left.

beats.say: The c on top and the c below cancel each other, leaving a b.
Put the number and the letters together: 13 a b.
Check by multiplying back. 13 times 7 is 91, and a b times c is a b c. So 13 a b times 7 c really is 91 a b c.
So to find a missing divider, divide by the answer instead. Numbers with numbers, and cancel matching letters.
A man bought some articles, counted in dozens. One of these decimals cannot be right. Which?

board.text: Dozens of articles: which one is impossible?

beats.say: You can only buy whole articles. So when we turn the dozens into single articles, the answer must be a whole number. How do we turn dozens into articles?

ask.ifNot: Each dozen is 12 articles. So the number of articles is the number of dozens times 12.

beats.say: The 3 whole dozens are fine in every choice: that is 36 articles. So only the part after the point needs testing.
0.75 of a dozen is three quarters of 12, which is 9. Whole. 0.25 is a quarter of 12, which is 3. Whole. And 0.5 is half of 12, which is 6. Whole.
Now the last one, 0.15 of a dozen. Will that be a whole number of articles? Have a guess before we work it out.
0.15 times 12 comes to 1.8. Nobody can buy 1.8 of an article!
So 3.15 dozen would mean 37.8 articles, and that cannot happen. 3.15 is the impossible one.
A count of things must be whole. Change the dozens into single items, and see whether it comes out whole.

spec.note: Perimeter = 16a + 7b

beats.say: The perimeter of an equilateral triangle is written with letters: 16 a plus 7 b. We are told a is 2 and b is 4, and we want one side.

ask.ifNot: A number written right next to a letter means times. So 16 a is 16 times 2.

beats.say: First we turn the perimeter into a real number. What does 16 a mean when a is 2?
16 a is 16 times 2, which is 32. And 7 b is 7 times 4, which is 28.

spec.note: Perimeter = 60

beats.say: Add the two pieces. 32 plus 28 is 60. So the perimeter, the walk all the way round, is 60.

ask.ifNot: Equilateral means all 3 sides of the triangle are equal. So the 60 is shared into 3 equal parts.

beats.say: Now, the triangle is equilateral. So how do we get one side from 60?
3 equal sides share the 60. 60 divided by 3 is 20. So each side is 20.
Check the walk: 20 plus 20 plus 20 makes 60. It fits.
So: put the numbers in place of the letters to get the perimeter, then share it among the 3 equal sides.
An article is priced at 800 rupees, and it is sold at a discount of 20 per cent. We want the sale price.
A discount is money taken off the price. So the sale price is the shorter bar, and the gap between the two is the discount.
First we need the discount in rupees. It is 20 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: The discount is taken off the price on the article. So it is 20 per cent of 800.

beats.say: 10 per cent of 800 is 80. So 20 per cent is 2 times 80, which is 160. The discount is 160 rupees.
Is 160 the sale price?

ask.ifNot: 160 rupees is what comes off. The sale price is what is left of the 800 after the discount is taken away.

beats.say: 800 minus 160 is 640. So the sale price is 640 rupees.
Check it another way. With 20 per cent off, you pay the other 80 per cent. That is 8 lots of 80, which is 640. Same answer.
So for a discount: find the per cent of the price, then take it away.
4000 rupees is to double, at 12.5 per cent simple interest. How many years will that take?
The 4000 rupees must double. So how much interest has to be earned?

ask.ifNot: Double 4000 is 8000. But the money starts at 4000, so the interest only has to bring in another 4000.

beats.say: Double 4000 is 8000. Take away the 4000 we began with, and the interest needed is 4000 rupees.

spec.note: To double, the interest must equal the start

beats.say: Now one year, at 12.5 per cent. Start with 10 per cent of 4000, which is 400.
The other 2.5 per cent is a quarter of 10 per cent. A quarter of 400 is 100. So one year earns 400 plus 100, which is 500 rupees.
Each year adds 500 rupees. How many years to reach 4000? 4000 divided by 500 is 8.
Here is a lovely way to check. 8 times 12.5 is 100. So in 8 years the interest reaches 100 per cent of the money: the whole sum again.
So for doubling: the interest must equal the starting money. Find one year's interest, and divide.
A three-digit number ending in 7, times a two-digit number ending in 8. Clubs hide the other digits. Which choice can be the product?
We can see only the last digits, 7 and 8. What must the product end in?

ask.ifNot: The last digit of a product comes from the last digits multiplied together. Work out 7 times 8, and look at the digit it ends in.

beats.say: 7 times 8 is 56, so the product ends in 6. That removes 29405, which ends in 5.
Three are left, all ending in 6. So test the size. The smallest numbers that fit are 107 and 18, and 107 times 18 is 1926.
1906 is smaller than that, so it is out. Only just, but out.
The biggest numbers that fit are 997 and 98. 997 times 98 is 97706. So what about 977706?

ask.ifNot: Count the digits. The biggest possible product, 97706, has five digits. 977706 has six, so it is far too big.

beats.say: Cross out 977706. Only 52606 is left, and it does work: 907 times 58 is 52606.
Last digit first, then smallest and biggest. Those two tests sort out almost every hidden-digit product.

board.text: (x + 37) is even. The 17th odd number before it?

beats.say: This one looks like algebra, but it is really about counting along a line of numbers.
We do not know x, and we do not need to. Think of x plus 37 as one even number, and walk backwards from it.

ask.ifNot: Even and odd numbers take turns. So the number right next to it, 1 less, is odd.

beats.say: What is the first odd number before any even number?
So the 1st one is 1 less. After that, each new odd number is 2 further back: 3 away, then 5 away.
To get from the 1st to the 17th takes 16 more jumps of 2. Careful: 16 jumps, not 17, because the 1st one is already counted.
16 jumps of 2 cover 32. Add the first step of 1, and we have gone 33 in all.
So the 17th odd number is 33 less than our starting number, x plus 37.
Plus 37, then minus 33, leaves plus 4. So we have x plus 4.
Try it with a real number. If x is 3, then x plus 37 is 40. Going back by 33 lands on 7. And 3 plus 4 is 7 too.
So the answer is x plus 4. Remember: 1 step to reach the first one, then jumps of 2 for all the rest.
We want the square of 125. That is a big one, so let's be sure what it means first.
A square number is a square of tiles. 5 squared is 5 rows of 5: 25 tiles. 125 squared is the same idea, just far too big to draw: 125 rows of 125.
So which sum is 125 squared?

ask.ifNot: Squared means times itself, not times 2. So it is 125 times 125.

beats.say: To multiply, we break the second 125 into 100, 20 and 5.
125 times 100 is 12500. 125 times 20 is 2500. And 125 times 5 is 625.
Now add the pieces. Start with 12500 plus 2500. What is that?

ask.ifNot: Add the thousands and the hundreds separately, and don't lose the carry. It comes to 15000.

beats.say: 12500 plus 2500 is 15000. And 625 more makes 15625.
So the square of 125 is 15625.
Here is a neat pattern for squaring a number that ends in 5. Take the 12, multiply by the next number, 13, to get 156. Then write 25 after it: 15625.
Squaring means multiplying a number by itself. Break it into easy pieces, and add the pieces carefully.
There are 5 tests, each out of 80 marks. A student has 30 per cent on the first 4. He wants 35 per cent over all 5. What must he score in the 5th test?

board.text: 5 tests of 80 marks. 30% in the first 4.

beats.say: Lots of numbers, so let us put them in a table. We need the marks he has from the first 4 tests, and the marks he wants from all 5.
All 5 tests are out of 5 times 80, which is 400 marks. The first 4 tests are out of 4 times 80, which is 320.
He wants 35 per cent of 400. Per cent means out of every 100, and 400 is 4 hundreds. 4 times 35 is 140 marks.
Now the marks he already has. He scored 30 per cent, but of which total?

ask.ifNot: He scored 30 per cent in the first 4 tests only. Those 4 tests are out of 320 marks.

beats.say: 10 per cent of 320 is 32. So 30 per cent is 3 times 32, which is 96. He has 96 marks so far.
He needs 140 and he has 96. The 5th test must give the difference: 140 minus 96 is 44.
Check: 96 plus 44 is 140, and 140 out of 400 is 35 for every 100. That is 35 per cent.
So for a target per cent: find the marks needed in total, find the marks already scored, and subtract.
A train 100 metres long runs at 36 kilometres per hour. How long does it take to pass a man standing by the rails?
To pass the man, the whole train has to go by him, front to back. So the train must travel its own length: 100 metres.
The distance is in metres and the choices are in seconds. But the speed is in kilometres per hour. Which units should the speed be in?

choices: leave it in km per hour
ask.ifNot: We want metres to match the train, and seconds to match the answer. So we change the speed into metres per second.

beats.say: In 1 hour the train goes 36 kilometres. 1 kilometre is 1000 metres, so that is 36000 metres.
And 1 hour is 60 times 60 seconds, which is 3600 seconds. So the train goes 36000 metres in 3600 seconds.
36000 is 10 lots of 3600. So in each second the train goes 10 metres.
10 metres every second, and 100 metres to cover. How long does that take?

ask.ifNot: Each second the train moves 10 metres. Count how many lots of 10 fit into 100.

beats.say: 100 divided by 10 is 10. The train passes the man in 10 seconds.
The slip to watch for is dividing 100 by 36 straight away. That mixes metres with kilometres, and seconds with hours.
So match the units first: metres with metres, seconds with seconds. Then time is distance divided by speed.
This line is not true yet. We need to slip in one pair of brackets so that it really equals 40.
As it stands, 3 times 25 is 75, and 75 minus 13 plus 4 is 66. Too big. So the brackets must bring it down.
Let's think backwards from 40. If the plus 4 comes last, then just before it we had 36. And 36 is 3 times what?

ask.ifNot: Go up the 3 times table. You reach 36 at 3 times 12.

beats.say: So we want the 3 to multiply 12. Can we make 12 from the numbers that follow? Yes: 25 minus 13 is 12. Put the brackets there.
Brackets first: 25 minus 13 is 12. Then times: 3 times 12 is 36.
And 36 plus 4 is 40. The line is true now.
The other choices do not work. Brackets round 3 times 25 change nothing. Round 13 plus 4 we get 58, and the long bracket gives 48.
To place brackets, work backwards from the answer you need, and look for the numbers that can make it.
We are told that 2 x, minus 3, equals 10. And we are asked for 4 x, minus 5. Notice the question never asks for x itself.
Start with the fact. How do we get the 2 x on its own?

ask.ifNot: The 2 x has a minus 3 with it. To undo minus 3 we do the opposite, and we do it to both sides.

beats.say: To undo minus 3 we add 3, on both sides. 10 plus 3 is 13. So 2 x equals 13.
We could divide by 2 now to find x. But look at what we need: 4 x. How is 4 x related to 2 x?

ask.ifNot: 4 is 2 times 2. So 4 x is 2 lots of 2 x. We do not even need to find x.

beats.say: So 4 x is double 13, which is 26.
Do not stop there! The question wants 4 x, minus 5. 26 minus 5 is 21.
We can check by finding x after all. 2 x is 13, so x is 13 divided by 2, which is 6.5. And 4 times 6.5, minus 5, gives 21 again.
The plan: find 2 x first, scale it up to 4 x, then finish with the minus 5. No need for x on its own.
Some number divides 167 and 95, and both times 5 is left over. Let's find it.
If dividing 167 leaves 5 over, which number does our divisor go into exactly?

ask.ifNot: Take away the 5 that was left over. What remains, 162, divides exactly.

beats.say: So our number divides 162 exactly. In the same way it divides 95 minus 5, which is 90.
Now split them into primes. 162 is even, so 2 comes out. The rest is four 3s.
And 90 is 2 times 3 times 3 times 5.
Which primes do 162 and 90 share?

ask.ifNot: Both have one 2. 162 has four 3s but 90 has only two, so two 3s are shared. The 5 is only in 90.

beats.say: Ring one 2 and two 3s on each line. Those are the primes both numbers have.
2 times 3 times 3 is 18, the biggest number that divides both. And a divisor must be bigger than its remainder: 18 is bigger than 5. So the number is 18.
Check. 167 is 18 times 9, plus 5. And 95 is 18 times 5, plus 5. Remainder 5 both times.
Same remainder each time? Take it off first, then find the H C F of what is left.

spec.note: Perimeter = 90 cm

beats.say: Here is a rectangle whose length is twice its breadth. The perimeter is 90 centimetres, and we want the area.
We do not know either side yet, so let's think in parts. Call the breadth 1 part. The length is twice as long, so it is 2 parts.

ask.ifNot: One length and one breadth make 3 parts, but that is only halfway round. The whole walk is 2 plus 1 plus 2 plus 1, which is 6 parts.

beats.say: Now walk all the way round the rectangle: a length, a breadth, another length, another breadth. How many parts is the whole walk?
The whole walk is 6 parts, and we know the walk is 90 centimetres. So 1 part is 90 divided by 6, which is 15 centimetres.
So the breadth, 1 part, is 15 centimetres. And the length, 2 parts, is 2 times 15, which is 30 centimetres.
Let's check the walk. 30 plus 15 is 45, and that is halfway. Double it: 45 plus 45 is 90. Just what we were told.

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides is for the walk round the edge. Area is rows of little squares, so we multiply the length by the breadth.

beats.say: Now for the area, the space inside. Which sum gives it?
30 times 15. Do 3 times 15 first: that is 45. Then make it 10 times bigger, and we have 450.
So the area is 450 square centimetres.
So: breadth 1 part, length 2 parts, the walk round 6 parts. One part from the perimeter gives both sides, and the sides give the area.
An article is sold for 407 rupees, and the shopkeeper makes a profit of 10 per cent. We want the cost price.
Two bars. The cost price is on top: call it 100 per cent. The selling price is longer, by the profit, which is 10 per cent of the cost price.
So the selling price, 407 rupees, is what per cent of the cost price?

ask.ifNot: The selling price is the whole cost price, 100 per cent, with the 10 per cent profit on top. That makes 110 per cent.

beats.say: Careful, here is the trap. Do not take 10 per cent of 407. The 10 per cent is of the cost price, and 407 is the selling price.
100 per cent plus 10 per cent is 110 per cent. That is 11 pieces of 10 per cent each, and together they are 407 rupees.
So one piece is 407 divided by 11. Try 37: 10 times 37 is 370, and one more 37 makes 407. So one piece is 37 rupees.
The cost price is 100 per cent, which is 10 of those pieces. 10 times 37 is 370.
Check: 10 per cent of 370 is 37, and 370 plus 37 is 407. It works.
So when you are given the selling price and the profit per cent, the selling price is 100 per cent plus the profit. Work back from there to the cost price.
Five decimals. We put them in descending order, biggest first, and then add the 1st and the 4th.
To compare decimals fairly, give them all the same number of decimal places. The longest have 3 places, so we pad the others with zeros.
Now every one is a number of thousandths. Which is the biggest?

ask.ifNot: Read them as thousandths: 62, 50, 560, 34 and 7. The biggest of those is 560, so 0.560 is the biggest decimal.

beats.say: Descending order means biggest first. So: 560, 62, 50, 34, 7 thousandths.
The 1st is 0.560, which is our 0.56. Count along to the 4th, and it is 0.034.
Add them. 560 thousandths plus 34 thousandths is 594 thousandths. That is 0.594.
The trap was to think 0.062 beats 0.56 because it has more digits. Line up the decimal places and that trap disappears.
To order decimals, pad them to the same length. Then compare them like whole numbers.
Some money earns 189 rupees of simple interest in 3 years, at 9 per cent per annum. We want that sum of money.

board.text: Interest Rs.189 in 3 years at 9% per annum

beats.say: Simple interest earns the same each year. So first, the interest for just one year: 189 divided by 3 is 63.
63 rupees is one year's interest, at 9 per cent. So 63 is 9 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: The rate is always a per cent of the money at the start. So 9 per cent of the sum is 63 rupees.

beats.say: 9 per cent of the sum is 63. So 1 per cent is 63 divided by 9, which is 7 rupees.
The whole sum is 100 per cent. 100 times 7 is 700. So the sum is 700 rupees.
Careful: the slip here is to forget the years, and treat 189 as one year's interest. Always bring it down to one year first.
Check: every 100 rupees earns 9, and 700 is 7 hundreds, so one year earns 63. 3 years earn 3 times 63, which is 189. It works.
So for the sum: interest for one year first, then 1 per cent, then 100 per cent.
We know a is 3 and b is 5, and c is made from them. Then we compare three expressions, to see which is greatest.
c first. c is b minus a, so 5 minus 3, which is 2.
Take the first expression: a plus c, in a bracket, times b. With the numbers in, that is 3 plus 2, times 5. What do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Brackets always come first. So we add 3 and 2 before we multiply.

beats.say: 3 plus 2 is 5, and 5 times 5 is 25.
The second one: a plus b, times c. 3 plus 5 is 8, and 8 times 2 is 16.
The third: b plus c, times a. 5 plus 2 is 7, and 7 times 3 is 21.
So the three values are 25, 16 and 21. The greatest is 25, and that came from a plus c, times b.
Notice they are not all equal, even though the same three numbers are used each time. So: find every letter, put the numbers in, do the brackets first, then compare.
A man walks 900 metres in 18 minutes. We want to know how far he walks in an hour.
18 minutes does not fit neatly into an hour, so let's use a stepping stone: 1 minute. How do we find how far he walks in 1 minute?

ask.ifNot: The 900 metres are spread evenly over 18 minutes. One minute's share is 900 split into 18 equal parts.

beats.say: 18 times 5 is 90, so 18 times 50 is 900. That means 900 divided by 18 is 50. He walks 50 metres every minute.
An hour is 60 minutes, so in an hour he walks 60 lots of 50 metres. 6 times 5 is 30, and two more zeros make 3000 metres.
The choices are in kilometres, so we are not finished. 1000 metres make 1 kilometre. What is 3000 metres in kilometres?

ask.ifNot: A kilometre is a bigger unit, so we need fewer of them. Count the thousands in 3000.

beats.say: 3000 divided by 1000 is 3. So he covers 3 kilometres in an hour.
Check the first step. 50 metres a minute, for 18 minutes, is 900 metres. That matches what we were told.
So: go down to 1 minute, build up to 60 minutes, and change the units at the end to match the choices.
Here we are not solving anything. We are translating a sentence into an equation, with m standing for a number.
Consecutive means next to each other. Here are some odd numbers in a row: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. How far apart are neighbours?

ask.ifNot: From 3 to 5 we jump over the 4. So odd numbers that are neighbours are always 2 apart.

beats.say: So if the first odd number is m, the next one is m plus 2.
The question says the sum of the two numbers is 16. What does the word sum tell us to do?

ask.ifNot: Sum is the answer to an addition. So we add the first number and the next number.

beats.say: So we add them, and that must equal 16. m, plus m plus 2, equals 16.
The other choices each miss something. m plus 2 equals 16 forgets the first number. 2 m treats the two numbers as equal. And m times m plus 2 multiplies, when sum means add.
Does our equation make sense? 7 and 9 are both odd, and they are neighbours. And 7 plus 9 is 16. It fits.
So the plan: give the first number a letter, build the second from it, and let the word sum tell you to add.
A captain has 850 soldiers. He wants as many soldiers in each row as there are rows. Some soldiers won't fit. How many?

board.text: 850 soldiers: soldiers in a row = number of rows

beats.say: As many in each row as there are rows: that makes a square. Here is a tiny parade, 4 rows of 4 soldiers, 16 in all.
The captain has 850 soldiers. Which square number does he need?

ask.ifNot: He cannot use more soldiers than he has, so the square cannot go above 850. To leave out as few as possible, he takes the biggest one that fits.

beats.say: 20 times 20 is 400: plenty of room left. 30 times 30 is 900: a little too many. So we step down just one from 30.
29 times 29. A quick way: 29 times 30 is 870, then take away one 29. That gives 841.
841 fits inside 850, and the next square, 900, does not. So he makes 29 rows of 29.
841 soldiers stand in the square. How many are left out?

ask.ifNot: Take the soldiers in the square away from all the soldiers: 850 minus 841.

beats.say: 850 minus 841 is 9. So 9 soldiers are left out.
Check: 29 rows of 29, plus the 9 left out, makes 850. Find the biggest square that fits, then subtract.
Five people eat 1 kilogram of rice in a day. How much rice will 20 people eat in a week?

board.text: 5 people eat 1 kg of rice in a day
20 people in a week eat ? kg

beats.say: Two things change here: the number of people, and the number of days. We will handle one at a time. People first.
Look at the bars. How many groups of 5 people are there in 20 people?

spec.note: Each group of 5 eats 1 kg in a day

ask.ifNot: Count in fives until you reach 20, and you will have counted 4 times. So there are 4 groups of 5 people.

beats.say: 20 divided by 5 is 4. Each group of 5 eats 1 kilogram a day, so 4 groups eat 4 kilograms a day.
That was for one day. Now, how many days are there in a week?

ask.ifNot: A whole week runs from Monday round to Sunday. That is 7 days, not just the school days.

beats.say: 4 kilograms each day, for 7 days. 4 times 7 is 28.
So 20 people eat 28 kilograms of rice in a week.
Check it the other way round. One group of 5 eats 7 kilograms in a week. 4 such groups eat 7 times 4, which is 28.
When two things change, change one at a time. First the people, then the days.
This line is not true as it stands. One pair of brackets will make it equal 33.
Without brackets, times goes first. 7 times 5 is 35, and 12 minus 35 already drops below zero. Nowhere near 33.
So think backwards from 33. If the plus 8 comes last, then just before it we had 25. And 25 is 5 times what?

ask.ifNot: 5 times 5 is 25. So we need a 5 to be sitting in front of the times 5.

beats.say: We need a 5 in front of the times 5. And look: 12 minus 7 is 5! So the brackets go round 12 minus 7.
Brackets first: 12 minus 7 is 5. Then 5 times 5 is 25.
And 25 plus 8 is 33. The line is true now.
What about the other choices? Brackets round 7 times 5 change nothing. The other two only make the amount we subtract bigger, so they sink below zero as well.
To place brackets, work backwards from the answer, and see which numbers can build what you need.
Which fraction is worth the same as 36 over 54? The choices are 14 over 21, 15 over 24, 6 over 14 and 7 over 18.
Here is the trick. Write every fraction in its simplest form. Then equal fractions look exactly the same.
Start with 36 over 54. What is the biggest number that divides both 36 and 54?

ask.ifNot: 6 and 9 both work, but we can go bigger. 18 times 2 is 36, and 18 times 3 is 54.

beats.say: Divide the top and the bottom by 18. 36 divided by 18 is 2, and 54 divided by 18 is 3. So 36 over 54 is really two thirds.
Now 14 over 21. 7 goes into both. 14 divided by 7 is 2, and 21 divided by 7 is 3. Two thirds again!
Let's be sure about the others. 15 over 24 is 5 over 8. 6 over 14 is 3 over 7. And 7 over 18 cannot be made any simpler.
None of those is two thirds. So the match is 14 over 21.
So to spot equal fractions: simplify each one. If they shrink to the same fraction, they are equal.

board.text: Supplement of an obtuse angle is always ...?

beats.say: Here is an obtuse angle on a straight line, with its supplementary angle beside it. What kind of angle will that partner always be?
First, the names. An obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle, 90 degrees, but smaller than a straight line, 180 degrees.
And supplementary angles share a straight line, so the two of them make 180 degrees together.
Let's try a real one. Say the obtuse angle is 120 degrees. Its supplement is 180 take away 120, which is 60 degrees.

ask.ifNot: The line holds 180 degrees, which is 2 lots of 90. If one angle takes more than 90, there must be less than 90 left over.

beats.say: Now think about every obtuse angle. It takes up more than 90 of the 180 degrees on the line. So how much is left for its partner?
There is always less than 90 left. Even a huge obtuse angle like 170 degrees leaves 10 degrees, which is still less than 90.
And an angle that is less than 90 degrees has a name: an acute angle. So the supplement of an obtuse angle is always acute.
So on a straight line, a big angle always has a small partner. Obtuse goes with acute, and a right angle goes with a right angle.
A basket of 104 mangoes. Again and again we take out 4 mangoes and put in 3 apples, until no mangoes are left. How many apples then?

board.text: 104 mangoes. Each swap: 4 mangoes out, 3 apples in

beats.say: First, how many swaps does it take to clear out all the mangoes?

ask.ifNot: Each swap removes 4 mangoes. So we need to know how many 4s there are in 104, and that is a division.

beats.say: 100 divided by 4 is 25, and the 4 that is left makes one more group. So 104 divided by 4 is 26 swaps.
Every swap puts 3 apples in. So how do we find the number of apples?

ask.ifNot: There are 26 swaps, and each one adds 3 apples. That is 26 lots of 3.

beats.say: 26 times 3. 20 times 3 is 60, 6 times 3 is 18, and together that is 78 apples.
Does 78 make sense? Yes. Only 3 apples go in for every 4 mangoes that come out, so there should be fewer apples than there were mangoes.
Count the swaps first, by dividing. Then multiply by what each swap brings in.
We want the 27th even number that comes after 27.

ask.ifNot: Odd and even numbers take turns. One more than 27 is 28, and 28 is even.

beats.say: 27 is odd. So what is the first even number after it?
So the list starts 28, 30, 32, 34 and carries on in jumps of 2.
28 is the 1st. To reach the 27th we need 26 more jumps. Careful: 26, not 27, because 28 itself is already counted.
26 jumps of 2 cover 52.
28 plus 52 is 80.
A quick test of the method on a small case: the 2nd even number should be 28 plus 1 jump, which is 30. Yes, it is.
So the 27th even number after 27 is 80. Find the first one, then add one jump fewer than the position.
A five litre can of liquid soap costs 370 rupees. What would a three litre can of the same soap cost?

board.text: A 5 litre can of soap costs ₹370

beats.say: Less soap, so it must cost less than 370 rupees. Keep that in mind as a safety check.
5 litres to 3 litres is an awkward jump. What do we find first?

ask.ifNot: Find one first. Once we know the cost of 1 litre, 3 litres is easy.

beats.say: 370 rupees shared over 5 litres. 370 divided by 5 is 74. So 1 litre costs 74 rupees.
And how do we get the cost of 3 litres?

ask.ifNot: 3 litres, at 74 rupees for each litre. 3 lots of 74 means multiply.

beats.say: 3 times 70 is 210, and 3 times 4 is 12. 210 plus 12 is 222.
So the three litre can costs 222 rupees.
Check. The other 2 litres would cost 2 times 74, which is 148. And 222 plus 148 is 370, the price of the full 5 litres.
The trap is to stop at 74, which is only 1 litre. Find one, then find many.
40 per cent of the students passed, and 420 students did not. We want the number of students who took the exam.
All the students together are 100 per cent. Let us draw them as one bar, cut into 10 equal pieces of 10 per cent each.

spec.note: 4 pieces passed, 6 pieces did not

beats.say: 420 is the number who did not pass. What per cent of the students is that?

ask.ifNot: 40 per cent passed. The rest did not, and the rest is 100 minus 40, which is 60 per cent.

beats.say: Careful, here is the trap. 420 is not the 40 per cent. It is the other part: 100 minus 40, which is 60 per cent.
60 per cent is 6 of our 10 pieces. So one piece is 420 divided by 6, which is 70.
All the students are 10 pieces. 10 times 70 is 700.
Check: one piece is 70, so the 4 pieces who passed are 280. And 700 minus 280 is 420, the ones who did not pass. It works.
So first ask: which per cent does my number really stand for? Then find one piece, and build up to the whole 100 per cent.
How many three-digit numbers can be divided by 4, by 5 and by 6? Such a number is a multiple of their L C M, so we find that first.

board.text: 3-digit numbers divisible by 4, 5 and 6: how many?

beats.say: Split each into primes. 4 is 2 times 2. 5 is prime. 6 is 2 times 3.
Take each prime the most times it appears: two 2s from 4, the 5, and the 3 from 6. 2 times 2 times 3 times 5 is 60.
So we are counting multiples of 60. Three-digit numbers start at 100. What is the first three-digit multiple of 60?

ask.ifNot: 60 has only two digits, and 100 is not in the 60 times table. The next multiple after 60 is 60 plus 60, which is 120.

beats.say: 120 is 60 times 2. So the first one is number 2 in the table.
Now the last one. 60 times 16 is 960. One more 60 would make 1020, which has four digits. So 960 is the last, number 16 in the table.
From number 2 in the table to number 16. How many numbers is that?

ask.ifNot: Out of 16 multiples, only the 1st one, 60 itself, is missing. 16 take away 1 is 15.

beats.say: 16 minus 2, plus 1 for counting both ends, is 15.
So: find the L C M, find its first and last multiple in the range, subtract their places in the table, and add 1.
Our angle is not a plain number this time. It is 35 minus x degrees, all in one bracket. We want its complementary angle.

ask.ifNot: A right angle is a quarter turn, and a quarter turn is 90 degrees. 180 is for a straight line.

beats.say: Complementary angles fit together in a square corner, a right angle. So what do the two of them add up to?
A right angle is 90 degrees. So the partner is 90 take away our angle. And our angle is the whole bracket, so the whole bracket is taken away.

ask.ifNot: The angle is 35 with x already taken off, so it is smaller than 35. Take a smaller angle from 90 and more is left over. So the x comes back as plus x.

beats.say: Taking the bracket away takes away the 35. But what happens to the minus x inside?
Careful here: the minus in front of the bracket reaches both things inside. The 35 becomes minus 35, and the minus x becomes plus x.
Now tidy up. 90 take away 35 is 55. So we have 55 plus x.
So the complementary angle is 55 plus x degrees, written in a bracket.
Check by adding the two angles. The minus x and the plus x cancel, and 35 plus 55 is 90. A perfect right angle.
The slip to watch for is leaving the sign alone and writing 55 minus x. Taking away a bracket flips the signs inside it.
Which is the smallest: 11 over 12, 10 over 11, 21 over 22, or 7 over 6?
One of these is bigger than 1 whole, so it cannot be the smallest. Which one?

ask.ifNot: Look for a top that is bigger than its bottom. In 7 over 6 the top is bigger, so it is more than 1 whole.

beats.say: 7 over 6 is out. The other three are special: each is just one piece short of a whole.
11 over 12 is 1 over 12 short of a whole. 10 over 11 is 1 over 11 short. And 21 over 22 is 1 over 22 short.
The smallest fraction is the one with the biggest piece missing. Which missing piece is the biggest?

ask.ifNot: Cut a bar into fewer pieces and each piece is bigger. 11 pieces is the fewest, so 1 over 11 is the biggest piece.

beats.say: 1 over 11 is the biggest gap. So 10 over 11 is the furthest from a whole, and that makes it the smallest.
When fractions are each one piece short of a whole, compare the missing pieces. The biggest gap gives the smallest fraction.

board.text: digits 2, 3, 4, 5: numbers with 5 in the hundreds

beats.say: All the 4 digit numbers made from 2, 3, 4 and 5, each used once. In how many is the 5 in the hundreds place?
Let's pin the 5 where it has to be. The hundreds place is taken, and three places are still empty.

ask.ifNot: Each digit is used only once, and the 5 is already taken. So only 2, 3 and 4 are left.

beats.say: Which digits are left to fill the empty places?
For the thousands place we can pick any of the 3. Then 2 are left for the tens, and 1 for the units.
Let's list them: 2534, 2543, 3524, 3542, 4523, 4532. Every one has 5 in the hundreds place.
So there are 6 such numbers.
Pin down the place that is decided. Then count the choices for the others and multiply.
Here is an equation with fractions. m plus 6, all over 11, equals m over 9. Fractions are awkward, so first we get rid of them.
Whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. If we multiply both sides by 11 and by 9, both bottoms disappear. People call this cross multiplying.
Now open the bracket. What does the 9 multiply?

ask.ifNot: The 9 is outside the bracket, so it multiplies everything inside: the m, and the 6 as well.

beats.say: 9 times m is 9 m, and 9 times 6 is 54.
m is on both sides. Take the smaller lot, 9 m, away from both sides. On the right, 11 m take away 9 m leaves 2 m.
54 equals 2 m. How do we find one m?

ask.ifNot: 2 m means 2 times m. Divide undoes times, so we halve both sides.

beats.say: Half of 54 is 27. So m equals 27.
Put 27 back. On the left, 27 plus 6 is 33, and 33 over 11 is 3. On the right, 27 over 9 is 3. Both sides are 3.
With a fraction on each side, cross multiply to clear the bottoms. After that it is an ordinary equation.

board.text: Square: side 15 cm. Rectangle: length 25 cm.

beats.say: A square has a side of 15 centimetres. A rectangle with a length of 25 centimetres has the same area. We want the difference between their perimeters.
Start with what we can find: the area of the square, side times side. For 15 times 15, split one 15 into 10 and 5. 15 times 10 is 150.
And 15 times 5 is 75. Together, 150 plus 75 makes 225. So the square's area is 225 square centimetres.

ask.ifNot: Area is length times breadth. So to get back from the area to the breadth, we divide by the length.

beats.say: The rectangle has the same area, 225, and its length is 25. How do we find its breadth?
225 divided by 25 is 9, because 9 times 25 is 225. So the breadth is 9 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: 25 plus 9 is only one length and one breadth, which is halfway round. We have to double it for the whole walk.

beats.say: Now the rectangle's perimeter, the walk all the way round. Which sum gives it?
25 plus 9 is 34, and that is halfway. Double it: the rectangle's perimeter is 68 centimetres.
The square's perimeter is easier: 4 equal sides of 15. 4 times 15 is 60 centimetres.
The difference is 68 take away 60, which is 8 centimetres.
Here is something worth noticing. The two shapes cover the same space, but the long thin one has the longer edge. Same area does not mean same perimeter.
A car drives at 72 kilometres per hour. We want to know how long it takes to cover 18 kilometres.

spec.note: 72 km in every hour

beats.say: 72 kilometres per hour means 72 kilometres in 1 hour. Our trip is only 18 kilometres, much less than that. So the time will be just a part of an hour.
So, what part of 72 is 18?

ask.ifNot: Try doubling. Double 18 is not yet 72, but double it again and you are there. So it takes 4 lots of 18, and 18 is one quarter of 72.

beats.say: 18 times 4 is 72. So 18 kilometres is one quarter of what the car does in an hour, and it needs one quarter of an hour.
The choices are in minutes, and 1 hour is 60 minutes. So how long is a quarter of an hour?

ask.ifNot: A quarter means one of 4 equal parts. Split the 60 minutes into 4 equal parts.

beats.say: 60 divided by 4 is 15. So the car takes 15 minutes.
Check it. 4 quarter hours make 1 hour, and 4 lots of 18 kilometres make 72 kilometres. That is exactly the speed we were given.
So time is distance divided by speed. When that comes out as a part of an hour, turn it into minutes using 60.

board.text: E = side of equilateral triangle, S = side of square

beats.say: E is the side of an equilateral triangle, and S is the side of a square. We have to find the pair where the two shapes have the same perimeter.

ask.ifNot: A square has 4 equal sides, so its walk round is 4 times S. S times S would be the space inside, the area.

beats.say: The triangle has 3 equal sides, so its walk round is 3 times E. What is the walk round the square?
The square has 4 equal sides, so its perimeter is 4 times S. Now we test each pair.
First pair: E is 9 and S is 9. 3 times 9 is 27, but 4 times 9 is 36. Not equal.
Second pair: E is 8 and S is 9. 3 times 8 is 24, and the square is still 36. Not equal.

ask.ifNot: The triangle has only 3 sides to make the same walk that the square makes with 4. So each of the triangle's sides has to be longer.

beats.say: Notice something. The square has more sides to walk along. So for the two walks to match, which side has to be the longer one?
The triangle's side has to be longer. Try E is 12 and S is 10. 3 times 12 is 36, but 4 times 10 is 40. Close, but not equal.
Last pair: E is 16 and S is 12. 3 times 16 is 48, and 4 times 12 is 48. Equal!
So the perimeters are equal when E is 16 and S is 12.
So when the choices are given, write the rule for each shape, then test the pairs one by one until both sides match.
A student scored 72 per cent on a test of 25 questions. We want the number of answers that were not correct.
72 per cent means 72 right out of every 100. But this test has only 25 questions, and 25 is one quarter of 100.
100 questions would give 72 right. This test is a quarter of that size. So how many did he get right?

ask.ifNot: A quarter of the questions means a quarter of the right answers. And to find a quarter, we divide by 4.

beats.say: To divide by 4, halve and halve again. Half of 72 is 36, and half of 36 is 18. So he got 18 answers right.
Careful now. Is 18 our answer?

choices: No: we want the ones not correct
ask.ifNot: 18 is the number he got right. The question asks for the answers that were not correct: the rest of the 25.

beats.say: 25 questions, 18 right. 25 minus 18 is 7. So 7 answers were not correct.
Check it another way. 100 minus 72 is 28, so 28 per cent were not correct. A quarter of 28 is 7. Same answer.
So read to the very end. Find the per cent, then check whether the question wants that part, or the rest.
A round bracket inside a curly bracket, and then a little minus 4 on the end.
What is the very first thing to work out?

ask.ifNot: We start inside the innermost bracket. And in there, times goes before plus. So 2 times 6 is the very first step.

beats.say: 2 times 6 is 12. Then 4 plus 12 is 16. The round bracket is done.
Now the curly bracket. 16 divided by 4 is 4.
And 4 minus 4 is 0.
Here is the trap they set. Adding 4 and 2 first gives 6 times 6, which is 36. Carry on from there and you reach 5, which is one of the choices!
Inside a bracket the same order still applies: times and divide before plus and minus. Then move outwards, bracket by bracket.
We want to write 12 minutes as a decimal part of an hour.
First as a fraction. 12 minutes is what fraction of an hour?

ask.ifNot: An hour has 60 minutes, not 100. So 12 minutes is 12 out of 60.

beats.say: 12 goes into 60 exactly 5 times. So 12 minutes is one fifth of an hour.
Now one fifth as a decimal. Decimals like tenths, so change it: one fifth is the same as 2 tenths, and 2 tenths is 0.2.
The choices show it as 0.20. That is the same number: a zero on the end of a decimal changes nothing.
Check: 0.2 of 60 minutes is 12 minutes. Yes.
The tempting slip is to write the 12 straight after the point. But minutes are sixtieths of an hour, so always divide by 60.
The 3 angles of this triangle are written with x. They are x, x plus 10, and 2 x minus 6. We want the greatest angle.

ask.ifNot: Tear the corners off a paper triangle and line them up. They make a straight line, a half turn. That is 180 degrees.

beats.say: We cannot compare the angles until we know x. So what do we know about the 3 angles of any triangle?
The 3 angles add up to 180 degrees. So we add ours and set the total equal to 180.
Gather the x's: 1 x, another x, and 2 x make 4 x. Then the plain numbers: plus 10 and minus 6 together make plus 4.
Take 4 away from both sides. 180 take away 4 leaves 176.
Divide both sides by 4, by halving twice. Half of 176 is 88, and half of 88 is 44. So x equals 44.

choices: Not yet: work out all 3 angles
ask.ifNot: x is only one of the angles. We have to work out the other two before we can say which is the greatest.

beats.say: x is 44. Is 44 degrees the greatest angle?
The first angle is 44 degrees. The second is 44 plus 10, which is 54 degrees. The third is 2 times 44, minus 6, which is 82 degrees.
Check that they make a triangle: 44 plus 54 plus 82 is 180. Good.
The angles are 44, 54 and 82 degrees. So the greatest angle is 82 degrees.
Careful with the last angle: 2 times 44 is 88, but we still have to take away the 6. So: angles add up to 180, find x, then work out every angle.
A machine makes 150 toys in one minute. How many toys does it make in 18 seconds?
Look at the units of time. One is in minutes, the other in seconds. What must we do before anything else?

ask.ifNot: We can't compare minutes with seconds. So first we write 1 minute as 60 seconds.

beats.say: 1 minute is 60 seconds. So the machine makes 150 toys in 60 seconds.
Find one first. In 1 second it makes 150 divided by 60. That is 2.5, two and a half toys each second.
And in 18 seconds?

ask.ifNot: Two and a half toys every second, for 18 seconds. That is 18 lots of 2.5, so we multiply.

beats.say: 18 times 2 is 36. 18 times a half is 9. 36 plus 9 is 45.
So the machine makes 45 toys in 18 seconds.
Check another way. 6 seconds is a tenth of a minute, so it gives a tenth of 150, which is 15 toys. 18 seconds is 3 lots of 6, and 3 times 15 is 45.
So make the units match, find one, then find many.
Here is 75003064. We may shuffle its digits any way we like, to make the smallest number we can.
First sort the digits from smallest to biggest. There are three zeros, then 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7.

choices: No, it would lose a digit
ask.ifNot: A zero at the front is never written, so the number would become shorter. We need the smallest digit that is not zero.

beats.say: The smallest digit is 0. Can our number start with 0?
So 3 goes first.
Now the zeros are welcome. They go straight after the 3, in the biggest places left, where they keep the number small.
Then the rest in rising order: 4, 5, 6, 7. That makes 30004567.
Careful: 30405067 also starts with 3, but it spends a 4 in the lakhs place where a 0 could go. Ours is smaller.
So the smallest number is 30004567. Smallest digit that is not zero first, then the zeros, then the rest in order.
3200 rupees grows to 3680 rupees in 3 years, at simple interest. We want the rate of interest.

board.text: Rs.3200 amounts to Rs.3680 in 3 years

beats.say: 3680 rupees is called the amount. It is the 3200 rupees that was put in, with the interest on top.
So how do we find the interest?

ask.ifNot: The amount is the starting money and the interest together. Take the starting money away, and the interest is what is left.

beats.say: 3680 minus 3200 is 480. So the interest is 480 rupees, for all 3 years.
Careful: the rate is for one year, not for all 3. Simple interest is the same every year, so one year's interest is 480 divided by 3, which is 160.
The rate tells us what every 100 rupees earns in one year. 3200 divided by 100 is 32, so the money is 32 hundreds.

board.text: Rate = interest on each Rs.100 in 1 year

beats.say: 32 hundreds earn 160 rupees a year. 32 times 5 is 160, so each hundred earns 5 rupees.
Each 100 rupees earns 5 rupees a year. That is a rate of 5 per cent per annum.
Check with the formula: principal, times rate, times time, divided by 100. 3200 times 5 times 3, divided by 100, is 480. That is our interest.
So for the rate: amount minus principal gives the interest. Share it over the years, and then over the hundreds.
We need the H C F of 513 and 456: the biggest number that divides both. These are big numbers, so here is a clever shortcut.
If a number divides two numbers, it also divides the gap between them. For example, 5 goes into 35 and into 20, and it goes into their gap, 15, as well.
The gap here is 513 minus 456, which is 57. So the H C F must be a factor of 57.
The H C F is a factor of 57. What is the biggest it could possibly be?

ask.ifNot: The biggest factor of any number is the number itself. So the H C F is 57 at the most. Now we test whether 57 really divides both.

beats.say: Test it. 57 times 8 is 400 plus 56, which is 456. So 57 goes into 456 exactly.
And one more 57 gives 456 plus 57, which is 513. So 57 times 9 is 513.
57 divides both numbers, and nothing bigger can. So the H C F is 57.
What about 19? It divides both too, because 57 is 3 times 19. But it is not the highest.
When two numbers are close together, look at their gap. The H C F always divides the gap, so test the gap first.
We add the smallest number we can to 1325, and the result must be a square number.
We can only add, so the square must be above 1325. And we want the very first one above it.
30 times 30 is 900, and 40 times 40 is 1600. 1325 is in between, so the root is between 30 and 40.
Let's try 36. 36 times 30 is 1080, and 36 times 6 is 216. So 36 times 36 is 1296.
1296 is a square, but it is below 1325. So what next?

ask.ifNot: We can only add, so we need a square above 1325. 1296 is too small, and we go up to the next one.

beats.say: 37 times 37. 37 times 30 is 1110, and 37 times 7 is 259. Together, 1369. That is the first square above 1325.
How far is it from 1325 up to 1369?

ask.ifNot: Find the gap going up: 1369 minus 1325.

beats.say: 1369 minus 1325 is 44. The smallest number to add is 44.
Check: 1325 plus 44 is 1369, and that is 37 times 37. To add up to a square, always look for the first square above.
A shopkeeper buys a pen for 40 rupees: that is the cost price. He wants a profit of 25 per cent. What should the selling price be?
Two bars. The top one is the cost price, 40 rupees. The selling price is longer, and the extra bit on the end is the profit.
The profit is 25 per cent. But 25 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: Profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 40 rupees.

beats.say: Careful: profit per cent is always worked on the cost price. And 25 per cent is one quarter, because 4 lots of 25 make 100.
A quarter of 40: half of 40 is 20, and half of 20 is 10. So the profit is 10 rupees.
The profit is 10 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 40 plus 10 is 50. So he should sell the pen for 50 rupees.
Check: the selling price, 50, is 10 more than the cost price, 40. And 4 lots of 10 make 40, so 10 really is a quarter of it.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on.

board.text: Right-angled triangle: sides 9 cm, 40 cm, 41 cm

beats.say: Here is a right-angled triangle. Its 3 sides are 9 centimetres, 40 centimetres and 41 centimetres. We want its area.

ask.ifNot: The longest side, 41, is the slanting one, opposite the right angle. The two shorter sides, 9 and 40, make the square corner.

beats.say: For the area we need a base, and a height that stands straight up from it, at a right angle. So which two sides meet at the right angle?
The two shorter sides make the right angle. So the base is 40 and the height is 9. Now watch: I draw a rectangle around the triangle, 40 long and 9 tall.
The rectangle's area is base times height. 4 times 9 is 36, so 40 times 9 is 360.

ask.ifNot: Our triangle is only half of the rectangle. So we need half of 360.

beats.say: The slanting side cuts that rectangle into two equal triangles. So what is the area of ours?
The triangle is half of the rectangle. Half of 360 is 180. That is the rule: half of base times height.

spec.note: Area = 180 sq. cm

beats.say: So the area is 180 square centimetres.
Notice that we never used the 41. The longest side is not a base or a height here, so it plays no part in the area. And do not forget the half.
Here is 87459. We compare what the 7 is worth with what the 5 is worth.

ask.ifNot: Count from the right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands. So the 7 means 7 thousands.

beats.say: Find them in the chart. What is the 7 worth?
7 times 1000 is 7000. And the 5 is in the tens place, so it is worth 5 times 10, which is 50.

ask.ifNot: 1000 divided by 10 compares the columns only, and forgets the digits 7 and 5. We divide the full place values.

beats.say: 'How many times' is which sum?
7000 divided by 50. Cross a zero off each to make it easier: 700 divided by 5 is 140.
Check: 140 times 50 gives back 7000.
So the place value of the 7 is 140 times the place value of the 5.
The digits are different here, so comparing the columns alone is not enough. Always divide the full place values.
A college has girls and boys, in a commerce stream and a science stream. Lots of numbers, so let's take them one at a time.

board.text: Girls = 735, which is 145 less than the boys

beats.say: The girls are 145 less than the boys. So how do we find the number of boys?

ask.ifNot: The girls are the smaller group. So the boys are 145 more than the girls: start from 735 and add 145.

beats.say: 735 plus 145 is 880. There are 880 boys.
So the whole college is 880 boys plus 735 girls. That is 1615 students.
The commerce stream has 435 boys and 375 girls, which is 810 students.
Everyone who is not in commerce is in science. 1615 minus 810 is 805.
Let's check another way. Science boys: 880 minus 435 is 445. Science girls: 735 minus 375 is 360. And 445 plus 360 is 805.
In a long word problem, find one missing number at a time. And watch which group is the bigger one when you read less than.
The series goes 10, 12, 15, 20, 27. We want the 8th term. Let's write the jumps underneath.
From 10 to 12 is plus 2. From 12 to 15 is plus 3. What is the jump from 15 to 20?

ask.ifNot: 20 minus 15 is 5. So the jump is plus 5.

beats.say: Plus 5. And then 27 minus 20 gives plus 7.
The jumps are 2, 3, 5, 7. They do not grow evenly, but these four belong to a famous family. Which one?

ask.ifNot: 2 is not odd, so they are not the odd numbers. 2, 3, 5 and 7 are the first prime numbers: each has only two factors.

beats.say: Prime numbers! So the next jumps are the next primes. Not 9, because 9 is 3 times 3. They are 11, 13 and 17.
We have 5 terms and want the 8th, so 3 more jumps. 27 plus 11 is 38. That is the 6th term.
38 plus 13 is 51. That is the 7th term. Which jump comes last?

ask.ifNot: 15 is 3 times 5, so it is not prime. The prime after 13 is 17.

beats.say: 51 plus 17 is 68. So the 8th term is 68.
Here is the whole list. Count along it: 8 terms, ending on 68.
When the jumps look uneven, write them in a row. They may be a family you know, like the primes.
Two friends are sending messages. Arnav sends m messages every hour, for 5 hours. Pranav sends p every hour, for 4 hours. We want the total.

board.text: Arnav: m each hour, for 5 hours
Pranav: p each hour, for 4 hours

beats.say: Imagine m was 3. Then Arnav sends 3, and 3, and 3, and 3, and 3. That is 5 lots of 3.
So with m messages each hour, for 5 hours, how many does Arnav send?

ask.ifNot: m each hour for 5 hours is m, 5 times over. And 5 lots of m is written 5 m.

beats.say: 5 lots of m. We write that as 5 m.
Pranav is the same idea. p messages each hour for 4 hours is 4 lots of p, which is 4 p.
Total means add. Can we join 5 m and 4 p into one term, like 9 m p?

choices: No: m and p are different letters
ask.ifNot: m and p stand for different numbers, so they are not like terms. We can only write them side by side, with a plus between.

beats.say: So the total is 5 m plus 4 p.
Test it. Say m is 2 and p is 3. Arnav sends 10, Pranav sends 12, and that is 22 altogether. And 5 times 2, plus 4 times 3, is 22.
So so many each hour, for so many hours, means multiply. And different letters always stay apart.
20 per cent of an electricity bill is taken off, and 100 rupees is still to be paid. We want the bill before anything was taken off.

board.text: 20% is taken off the bill. Rs.100 is left to pay.

beats.say: The whole bill is 100 per cent. Cut it into 5 equal pieces, and each piece is 20 per cent.

spec.note: 1 piece is taken off, 4 pieces are left

beats.say: One piece, 20 per cent, is taken off. So the 100 rupees left to pay is what per cent of the bill?

ask.ifNot: 100 per cent, take away 20 per cent, leaves 80 per cent. The 100 rupees is that 80 per cent.

beats.say: Careful: the 100 rupees is not the whole bill, and it is not the 20 per cent either. It is the 80 per cent that is left: 4 of the 5 pieces.
4 pieces are 100 rupees. So one piece is 100 divided by 4, which is 25 rupees.
The whole bill is 5 pieces. 5 times 25 is 125. So the bill was 125 rupees.
Check: 20 per cent of 125 is one piece, 25 rupees. And 125 minus 25 is 100, just as the question says.
So when a part is taken off, work out what per cent is left, find one piece, and build the whole.

board.text: (x + 21) is odd. The 3rd even number after it?

beats.say: There is a letter in this one, but it is really a counting puzzle.
We do not know x, but we do know x plus 21 is odd. Let's walk forward from it, one number at a time.

ask.ifNot: Odd and even numbers take turns, like left foot, right foot. After an odd number comes an even one.

beats.say: What kind of number comes right after an odd number?
So the 1st even number is just 1 more: x plus 22.
Even numbers are 2 apart. So the 2nd one is x plus 24.
And the 3rd is x plus 26. Careful: the first step was only 1, because we started on an odd number. After that the steps are 2.
Try it with a real number. If x is 2, then x plus 21 is 23. The even numbers after 23 are 24, 26, 28. And 2 plus 26 is 28.
So the answer is x plus 26. One step to reach the first even number, then jumps of 2.
Four sums made from 10 and 3. This time we want the greatest, so let's work out each one.
Start with the first, 10 minus 3 times 3. Which part goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times comes before minus. So 3 times 3 goes first, even though the minus is on the left.

beats.say: 3 times 3 is 9, and 10 minus 9 is 1.
The second has a bracket, and brackets go first. 10 plus 3 is 13, and 13 times 3 is 39.
The third: 10 times 3 is 30, and 30 plus 3 is 33.
The fourth: 3 times 3 is 9, and 9 plus 10 is 19.
So the values are 1, 39, 33 and 19. The greatest is 39, from the one with the bracket.
See what the bracket did? It made the 3 multiply the whole of 10 plus 3, not just one number. Work each choice in the proper order, then compare.
Here the angle is written with a letter: x minus 35 degrees. We need the angle that is complementary to it.

ask.ifNot: A right angle is a quarter turn, and a quarter turn is 90 degrees. 180 is for a straight line.

beats.say: Complementary angles fit together in a square corner, a right angle. So what do the two of them add up to?
A right angle is 90 degrees. So the partner is 90 take away our angle. And our angle is the whole bracket, so the whole bracket is taken away.

ask.ifNot: The angle is x with 35 already taken off. Taking away an angle that is 35 smaller leaves 35 more. So the 35 comes back as plus 35.

beats.say: Taking the bracket away takes away the x. But what happens to the minus 35 inside?
Careful here: the minus in front of the bracket reaches both things inside. The x becomes minus x, and the minus 35 becomes plus 35.
Now tidy up. 90 plus 35 is 125. So we have 125 minus x.
So the complementary angle is 125 minus x degrees, written in a bracket.
Check by adding the two angles. The x and the minus x cancel, and 125 take away 35 is 90. A perfect right angle.
The slip to watch for is leaving the sign alone. Taking away a bracket flips the signs inside it, so minus 35 turns into plus 35.
A man earned 120 rupees by selling 8 dozen mangoes. How much would he earn by selling 20 dozen?
More dozens sold, more rupees earned. So our answer must be bigger than 120.
8 dozen to 20 dozen is not a neat jump. What should we find first?

ask.ifNot: Find one first. From the earning on 1 dozen, we can reach 20 dozen, or any number of dozens.

beats.say: 120 rupees from 8 dozen. 120 divided by 8 is 15. He earns 15 rupees on each dozen.
And for 20 dozen?

ask.ifNot: 20 dozens, each earning 15 rupees. 20 lots of 15 means multiply.

beats.say: 2 times 15 is 30, so 20 times 15 is 300.
He would earn 300 rupees.
Check by a different path. 4 dozen is half of 8 dozen, so it earns half of 120, which is 60. 20 dozen is 5 lots of 4 dozen, and 5 times 60 is 300.
Find one, then find many. And notice we stayed in dozens the whole way, because the question did.
A 4 by 4 grid of squares has 9 points inside where the lines cross. How many would a 16 by 16 grid have?
Here is the 4 by 4 grid. The dots are where the inside lines cross. Count them: 3 rows of 3 dots, 9 in all.
The grid is 4 squares wide, yet there are only 3 dots in a row. Why?

choices: the edge dots were left out
ask.ifNot: The dots sit on the lines between squares. 4 squares in a row have 3 lines between them, just as 4 fingers have 3 gaps.

beats.say: Test that on a smaller grid. A 3 by 3 grid has 2 rows of 2 dots: 4 dots.
Put it in a table. The dots in a row are always 1 fewer than the squares in a row.
So for a 16 by 16 grid, how many dots are in each row?

ask.ifNot: Always 1 fewer than the number of squares across. 16 squares have 15 gaps between them.

beats.say: 16 minus 1 is 15. So there are 15 dots in a row, and 15 rows of dots. That is 15 times 15.
15 tens are 150, and 15 fives are 75. Together, 225. So there are 225 points inside.
The trap is 16 times 16, which is 256. That counts the squares, not the crossing points. The points make a 15 by 15 square: 225.

board.text: Right-angled triangle: sides 7 cm, 24 cm, 25 cm

beats.say: Here is a right-angled triangle with sides of 7, 24 and 25 centimetres. This time we are not asked for the area itself, but for a calculation that gives it.

ask.ifNot: The longest side, 25, is the slanting one, opposite the right angle. The two shorter sides, 7 and 24, make the square corner.

beats.say: The area needs a base, and a height standing straight up from it. So which two sides meet at the right angle?
The two shorter sides make the right angle, so they are the base and the height. Draw the rectangle around the triangle: the triangle is exactly half of it.
So the area is half of base times height: a half, times 24, times 7.

ask.ifNot: The half is used only once. Halve the 24 to get 12, and leave the 7 alone.

beats.say: We can do the half straight away, on the 24. So which of these is the same calculation?
Half of 24 is 12, so the area is 12 times 7. And 12 times 7 is the same as 7 times 12.
So the calculation is 7 times 12.

spec.note: Area = 84 sq. cm

beats.say: 7 times 12 is 84 square centimetres. Look at the traps. 3.5 times 12 halves twice and gives only 42. And the 25 should never appear: the slanting side is neither base nor height.
So for a right-angled triangle: the two sides at the right angle are base and height, and the area is half of their product. Halve once, and only once.
Harry buys a saddle for 100 rupees, sells it for 200, buys it back for 300, and sells it again for 400. Did he make a profit or a loss overall?

board.text: Bought Rs.100, sold Rs.200, bought Rs.300, sold Rs.400

beats.say: Four deals, and it is easy to get muddled. So we make two columns: money Harry paid out, and money he got in.
To see how he did overall, what should we compare?

choices: all he paid with all he got
ask.ifNot: Every rupee counts. Add up everything he paid out, add up everything he got in, and then compare the two totals.

beats.say: Money paid out: 100 in April and 300 in June. 100 plus 300 is 400 rupees.
Money got in: 200 in May and 400 in July. 200 plus 400 is 600 rupees.
He got in more than he paid out, so it is a profit. 600 minus 400 is 200 rupees.
Careful with the trap here. Buying it back for 300, after selling it for 200, feels like losing 100. But the two columns tell the whole story.
Check it deal by deal. Bought at 100, sold at 200: a profit of 100. Bought at 300, sold at 400: another 100. And 100 plus 100 is 200.
So with many deals, total the money paid out, total the money got in, and compare the two.
Here is our equation. 3 x, plus 7, equals 1, minus 2 x. There is an x on each side, so let's bring them together.
On the right there is a minus 2 x. How do we move it over to the left side?

ask.ifNot: To undo minus 2 x, we add 2 x. And we add it to both sides, so the balance stays level.

beats.say: Add 2 x to both sides. On the right it cancels, leaving 1. On the left, 3 x plus 2 x makes 5 x.
Now undo the plus 7, by taking 7 from both sides.
1 minus 7. We have 1, and we take away 7. Where do we land?

ask.ifNot: Taking 7 from 1 takes us below zero. From 1 down to 0 is 1 step, then 6 more steps down. That lands on minus 6.

beats.say: So 5 x equals minus 6. The last move is the usual one: divide both sides by 5.
Minus 6 divided by 5 does not come out as a whole number, so we leave it as a fraction. x equals minus 6 over 5.
Check with the tidy line, 5 x plus 7 equals 1. 5 times minus 6 over 5 is minus 6. And minus 6 plus 7 is 1. It works.
The plan: letters to one side, numbers to the other, each time by doing the opposite to both sides. And an answer can be a negative fraction.
A fruit seller has apples, mangoes and oranges. We know three pair totals. First we find how many of each he has. Then he sells 100 of each.
Suppose we add all three totals together. How many times does each fruit get counted?

ask.ifNot: Look for A in the three lines: it appears in 2 of them. The same is true for M and for O. So every fruit is counted twice.

beats.say: The three totals add up to 1140. That counts every fruit twice, so we halve it. All the fruit together is 570.
All three make 570, and apples with mangoes make 400. Which fruit does that give us?

ask.ifNot: Take the apples and mangoes away from all the fruit, and only the oranges are left.

beats.say: So oranges are 570 minus 400, which is 170. In the same way, apples are 570 minus 300, which is 270. And mangoes are 570 minus 440, which is 130.
Do not stop here! He sells 100 of each. Apples go down to 170, mangoes to 30, and oranges to 70.
So he has 170 apples, 30 mangoes and 70 oranges left.
Check the starting numbers. 270 apples and 130 mangoes make 400. 130 mangoes and 170 oranges make 300. Both match the question.
So when every pair total is given: add them all, halve, then subtract each pair. And finish the story: 170, 30 and 70.

board.text: place value of 9 − place value of 7 = 83000

beats.say: Four numbers, each with a 9 and a 7. In one of them, the place values of the 9 and the 7 differ by 83000.

ask.ifNot: Try them. 90000 minus 7000 is 83000. The other pairs give differences that are too small or too big.

beats.say: Think first. Which two place values have a difference of 83000?
90000 minus 7000 is 83000. So the 9 must be worth 90000 and the 7 must be worth 7000.
That means 9 in the ten-thousands place, with 7 right beside it in the thousands place. Let's look for that pattern.
1907000: here the 9 is in the lakhs place, worth 900000. Far too much.
109700: the 9 is only worth 9000. And in 91700 the 9 is right, but the 7 is only worth 700. Both out.
197000: 9 in the ten-thousands, 7 in the thousands. Exactly what we wanted.
So the number is 197000. Working out what we needed first made the search quick.
Three bells beep every 2, 5 and 8 minutes. They all beeped together at 10:00 a.m., and we want the next time that happens.

board.text: Bells beep every 2, 5 and 8 minutes from 10:00 a.m.

beats.say: Each bell follows its own times table: the 2s, the 5s and the 8s. They beep together when the minutes are in all three tables.

board.text: Beeping together: a time in all three tables

beats.say: Which table should we count up in to find that fastest?

ask.ifNot: Any table would get there in the end. But the 8 times table has the fewest numbers to test, so it is the quickest.

beats.say: Count up in 8s: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40. All of these are even, so the 2 bell is always happy.
Now, which of them is in the 5 times table? It must end in 0 or 5. Only 40 does, and 40 is 5 times 8.
So the L C M of 2, 5 and 8 is 40. The bells beep together every 40 minutes.
They beeped together at 10:00 a.m. When is the next time?

ask.ifNot: The next time comes one L C M later. 40 minutes after 10:00 a.m. is 10:40 a.m.

beats.say: 40 minutes after 10 o'clock is 10:40 a.m.
Events that repeat come together again after the L C M of their gaps. Count up in the biggest table and test the others.
25 rupees is to become 37 rupees, at 16 per cent per annum simple interest. How long will it take?

board.text: Rs.25 becomes Rs.37 at 16% per annum

beats.say: 37 rupees is the amount: the 25 at the start, with the interest on top. The interest needed is 37 minus 25, which is 12 rupees.
Now the interest for one year. It is 16 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: Interest is always worked on the money at the start, the principal. That is 25 rupees.

beats.say: 16 per cent means 16 rupees on every 100. But 25 is only a quarter of 100. So it earns a quarter of 16, which is 4 rupees a year.
Each year adds 4 rupees, and we need 12. 12 divided by 4 is 3. So it takes 3 years.
Check it a year at a time, in the table. 25 grows to 29, then 33, then 37. After 3 years it reaches 37 rupees.
So for the time: find the interest needed, find the interest for one year, and divide.
5 over 8 of the teachers play chess, 3 over 8 play carrom, and one quarter play both. What fraction play neither game?
Let's draw two overlapping circles. The teachers who play both games sit in the middle, where the circles overlap.
If we add 5 over 8 and 3 over 8, how many times do the teachers in the middle get counted?

ask.ifNot: They play chess, so they are inside the 5 over 8. They also play carrom, so they are inside the 3 over 8 as well. That is twice.

beats.say: So we add chess and carrom, and then take the middle away once. 5 over 8 plus 3 over 8 is 8 over 8, which is 1.
Now take away the one quarter that we counted twice. 1 take away one quarter is three quarters. So three quarters of the teachers play at least one game.
Three quarters play something. So what fraction play nothing at all?

ask.ifNot: All the teachers together make 1 whole. If three quarters play a game, the rest is 1 take away three quarters.

beats.say: 1 take away three quarters is one quarter. So one quarter of the teachers play neither game.
The trap was the answer 0. 5 over 8 and 3 over 8 do add up to 1, but only because some teachers were counted twice.
When two groups overlap: add them, take the overlap away once, and whatever is left of the whole is neither.
An ant moves 15 feet every minute. We want to know how far it travels in 24 minutes and 40 seconds.
The time has two parts, whole minutes and some extra seconds. Let's take them one at a time, starting with the 24 whole minutes. What do we work out?

ask.ifNot: Every minute adds another 15 feet. 24 minutes means 24 lots of 15, so we multiply.

beats.say: 24 times 15 in two pieces. 24 times 10 is 240. 5 is half of 10, so 24 times 5 is half of 240, which is 120. Together, 360 feet.
Careful: 360 is one of the choices, and it is tempting to stop here. But the ant keeps walking for 40 more seconds.
The speed is per minute, so we need the 40 seconds as a part of a minute. A minute has 60 seconds. What part of a minute is 40 seconds?

ask.ifNot: A minute has 60 seconds, not a hundred, so 40 seconds is not 0.4 of a minute. 40 out of 60 is the same as 4 out of 6, which is two thirds.

beats.say: 40 out of 60 is two thirds. One third of 15 feet is 5 feet, so two thirds is 10 feet.
Now put the two parts together. 360 plus 10 is 370. The ant travels 370 feet.
Sense check. A full 25 minutes would be 375 feet. Our time is a little under 25 minutes, and 370 is a little under 375. It fits.
So when a time has minutes and seconds, work out each part on its own, and turn the seconds into a part of a minute using 60.
Krina meant to multiply by 2, but pressed times 20. We want one more step that puts it right.
Let's try it with a real number, so we can see what happened. Say her number was 7. She wanted 14, but the calculator shows 140.
140 instead of 14. How many times too big is her answer?

ask.ifNot: 20 is 10 times as big as 2. So her answer came out 10 times as big as it should be.

beats.say: To fix an answer that is 10 times too big, we divide by 10. But look at the choices: none of them says divide by 10!
Which of the choices does the same job as dividing by 10?

ask.ifNot: 0.1 is one tenth. Multiplying by one tenth means taking a tenth of the number, and that is exactly the same as dividing by 10.

beats.say: 140 times 0.1 is 14. So she should multiply by 0.1.
Why not divide by 20? That would undo the whole times 20 and leave just her starting number, 7. She still wants it doubled.
Remember: multiplying by 0.1 is the same as dividing by 10. And multiplying by 0.5 is the same as halving.
We are not told a or b. We only know that a divided by b is 2. Yet that is enough to find 4 b over a.
a divided by b is 2. What does that tell us about a and b?

ask.ifNot: 10 divided by 5 is 2, because 10 is 2 times 5. In the same way, a divided by b is 2 means a is 2 times b.

beats.say: So a is double b. Let's pick an easy pair that fits: b is 1 and a is 2.
Now work out 4 b over a. 4 times 1 is 4, and 4 divided by 2 is 2.
Was that luck? Try another pair: b is 3 and a is 6. 4 times 3 is 12, and 12 divided by 6 is 2 again.
Here is why it always works. If a over b is 2, what is b over a, the fraction flipped?

ask.ifNot: Flipping a fraction turns it upside down. 2 is 2 over 1, so upside down it is 1 over 2, a half.

beats.say: b over a is a half. And 4 b over a is 4 times that. 4 times a half is 2.
So when you only know how two letters compare, try easy numbers that fit, then look for the reason. The answer is 2.

board.text: two primes next to each other add up to 42

beats.say: Two prime numbers, next to each other in the list of primes, add up to 42. We want the difference between them.
If two numbers are close together and add up to 42, each must be close to half of 42. Half of 42 is 21.

ask.ifNot: 20 is even, so it is not prime. 19 cannot be divided by anything, so it is the nearest prime below 21.

beats.say: So one prime is a little below 21 and the other a little above. Which is the nearest prime below 21?
Here are the numbers around 21. Cross out 20 and 22, which are even, and 21, which is 3 times 7. The primes left are 19 and 23.
19 plus 23 is 42. It fits! And there is no prime between them, so they really are next to each other.
Now the difference. 23 minus 19 is 4.
So the two primes differ by 4.
When two numbers have a known total, start from half of it and look on both sides.
A man agrees to do a job in 30 days for 27,000 rupees. But he works for 18 days and then leaves. How much should he be paid?

board.text: He works only 18 days. Fair pay = ₹ ?

beats.say: What is fair? He should be paid for the days he worked, and not for the days he did not.
To pay him fairly, what should we find first?

ask.ifNot: The 27,000 rupees is for all 30 days. So first we find the pay for 1 day.

beats.say: 27,000 divided by 30 is 900, so one day of work earns 900 rupees. Careful: we divide by 30, the days the money was meant for, not by 18.
He worked 18 days. So what do we work out?

ask.ifNot: He earns 900 rupees for each day he worked, and he worked 18 days. So it is 18 times 900.

beats.say: 18 times 9 is 162, so 18 times 900 is 16,200.
A fair employer pays him 16,200 rupees.
Check. He missed 30 minus 18, that is 12 days, worth 12 times 900, which is 10,800 rupees. And 16,200 plus 10,800 is 27,000.
So for part of a job: find the pay for one day, then multiply by the days really worked.
We add the least number we can to 1300 and must land on a perfect square.
Adding moves us up the number line. So we need the first perfect square after 1300. A handy one to start from: 35 times 35 is 1225.
Here is a trick for stepping to the next square. A 3 by 3 square of tiles grows into a 4 by 4 square when we add a row of 3 and a column of 4.
So to get from 35 times 35 to 36 times 36, we add 35 and 36. 1225 plus 35 plus 36 is 1296.
1296 is only 4 short of 1300. Can we use it?

ask.ifNot: Adding can only make 1300 bigger. So a square below 1300 is no use to us. We go on to the next square.

beats.say: The same trick again: 1296 plus 36 plus 37 is 1369. So 37 times 37 is 1369, the first square above 1300.
How far is it from 1300 up to 1369?

ask.ifNot: Find the gap going up: 1369 minus 1300.

beats.say: 1369 minus 1300 is 69. The least number to add is 69.
Check: 1300 plus 69 is 1369, which is 37 times 37. The square just below was tempting, but adding can only take us up.
A square bracket with a round bracket inside it, and the little word of in the middle.
What is the very first thing to work out?

ask.ifNot: Innermost bracket first, and inside it times goes before minus. So 2 times 10 is the first step. Doing 25 minus 2 first is the classic slip.

beats.say: 2 times 10 is 20, and 25 minus 20 is 5. The round bracket is worth 5.
Now we meet 3 of 5. What does the word of tell us to do?

ask.ifNot: 3 of something means 3 lots of it. And lots of means multiply.

beats.say: 3 times 5 is 15. And of is done before the plus, just like times. So the square bracket is 5 plus 15, which is 20.
And 778 minus 20 is 758.
Brackets from the inside out. Inside each one, of and times and divide go first, then plus and minus.

board.text: Second: same area, length 16 cm. Width = ?

beats.say: The first rectangle is 12 centimetres long and 8 centimetres wide. A second rectangle has the same area, but it is 16 centimetres long. How wide is it?

ask.ifNot: The two rectangles have the same area, so the area is the bridge from the first one to the second.

beats.say: The two rectangles share one thing. So what should we work out first?
The area of the first rectangle is length times width. 12 times 8 is 96 square centimetres.

ask.ifNot: Area is length times width. So to get back from the area to the width, we divide by the length. Adding 4 to one side and taking 4 off the other does not keep the area the same.

beats.say: The second rectangle also covers 96 square centimetres, and it is 16 long. How do we find its width?
96 divided by 16 is 6, because 16 times 6 is 96. So the width is 6 centimetres.
So the second rectangle is 6 centimetres wide.
Notice what happened. The length grew from 12 to 16, so the width had to shrink from 8 to 6 to hold the same area. Same area: multiply for the first, divide for the second.
Ajay's sequence starts 3, 14, 25, 36. We must decide which bigger number could turn up in it later.
What is the jump from each number to the next?

ask.ifNot: 14 minus 3 is 11. 25 minus 14 is 11. 36 minus 25 is 11.

beats.say: Plus 11, every time.
So every number in the list is 3, plus some 11s. 14 is 3 plus one 11. 25 is 3 plus two 11s. 36 is 3 plus three 11s.
