The numbers start 8, 12, 16, and keep going. Our job is to find the 10th one without writing them all out.
First, see how it grows. What is the jump from each number to the next?

ask.ifNot: Subtract neighbours: 12 minus 8 is 4, and 16 minus 12 is 4 again. So the jump is plus 4.

beats.say: Plus 4, every single time. A sequence that climbs by the same jump each time is called an arithmetic sequence.
We can't write out all 10 terms, so let's count jumps instead. The 2nd term is 1 jump from the start. The 3rd term is 2 jumps.
See the pattern in the table? So how many jumps take us to the 10th term?

ask.ifNot: Look at the table again. The jumps are always 1 fewer than the term number, because the 1st term needs no jump at all. So the 10th term needs 9 jumps.

beats.say: 9 jumps, and each jump is 4. 9 times 4 is 36.
Now start at 8, the first term, and add all those jumps. 8 plus 36 is 44. So the 10th term is 44.
Let's test the idea on a term we already know. The 3rd term is 2 jumps from 8: 8 plus 2 times 4 is 16. And 16 is right there in our list.
The plan: find the jump, count the jumps, which is always 1 fewer than the term number, multiply, then add the first term.
We need to add up 3, 5, 7, and so on, all the way to 21. One by one would take ages, so let's be clever.
First, the jump. 5 minus 3 is 2, and 7 minus 5 is 2. So the numbers climb by 2 each time.
How many numbers are in the list? From 3 up to 21 is a climb of 18. In jumps of 2, that is 9 jumps.
9 jumps. So how many numbers are there?

ask.ifNot: Think of fence posts. 1 jump joins 2 numbers, and 2 jumps join 3 numbers. There is always 1 more number than jumps.

beats.say: 1 more than the jumps: 10 numbers in all.
Now the clever bit. Add the first and the last: 3 plus 21 is 24. Then the second and the second last: 5 plus 19 is 24 again!
Every pair makes 24. So write the list twice, once forwards and once backwards, and we get 10 pairs of 24. 10 times 24 is 240.
But 240 has every number counted twice. What do we do to get the real sum?

ask.ifNot: We wrote the list two times, so 240 is double the sum. Halving it brings us back.

beats.say: Half of 240 is 120. So the sum is 120.
Does the trick really work? Try just the first 3 numbers. 3 plus 5 plus 7 is 15. The trick says: 3 plus 7 is 10, times 3, then halved. That is 15 too.
So, to add a long, evenly spaced list: count the numbers, add the first and the last, multiply, and halve.
Look at this pattern: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. Something comes next, and the numbers themselves will tell us what.
Look at two neighbours at a time. What is the jump from each number to the next?

ask.ifNot: From 4 to 6 is 2 more. From 6 to 8 is 2 more again. The jump is plus 2.

beats.say: Plus 2, plus 2, plus 2, all the way along. The jump never changes.
The last number we have is 12. So what comes next?

ask.ifNot: Keep the very same jump. Start at 12 and go up 2 more.

beats.say: 12 plus 2 is 14. So the next number is 14.
Read the whole line back: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14. Every step is plus 2. It fits.
For any number pattern, look at the jumps between neighbours first. If they are all the same, make that jump once more.

board.text: From 1 to 51: how many are divisible by 9?

beats.say: From 1 to 51, some numbers can be divided by 9 exactly. Our job is to count them.
Divisible by 9 means the number is in the 9 times table. So really, we are counting multiples of 9.

ask.ifNot: 54 is past 51, and 36 is not the last one we can reach. The last multiple of 9 inside the range is 45.

beats.say: Let's find the far end first. Which is the last multiple of 9 that does not go past 51?
9 times 5 is 45. One more step gives 54, and that is past 51.
Look at the 9 times table from its very start. 45 is multiple number 5. So up to 51 there are 5 multiples of 9.
Do we lose any at the start? No. Our range begins at 1, and the first multiple, 9, is already inside. All 5 count.
Check by listing them: 9, 18, 27, 36, 45. Count them, and there are 5.
So 5 numbers from 1 to 51 are divisible by 9.
When the range starts at 1, just find the last multiple and see which number it is in the times table.

board.text: Sum of the first 15 natural numbers = ?

beats.say: The first 15 natural numbers, all added together. Adding them one by one is slow, so here is a smarter way.
Natural numbers are the counting numbers: 1, 2, 3 and so on. The first 15 of them end at 15.
Do not start adding from the left. Join the two ends instead: 1 plus 15 makes 16.

ask.ifNot: 2 plus 14 is 16 again. One number went up by 1 and the other came down by 1, so the total did not change.

beats.say: Now the second and the second last: 2 and 14. What do they make?
16 once more. Keep stepping inwards from both ends, and every pair makes 16.
15 is an odd count, so one number is left alone in the middle. It is half of 16, which is 8. The rest make 7 pairs.
7 pairs of 16, plus the middle 8, makes 120.
Check another way. Write the list twice, once forwards and once backwards. That makes 15 columns of 16, and half of that is 120.
So the sum of the first 15 natural numbers is 120.
Pair the ends, count the pairs, multiply. That trick turns a long sum into a short one.

From 11 to 49 is 38. Each jump is 2, so that is 19 jumps.

ask.ifNot: Think of fence posts. 1 jump joins 2 numbers, and 2 jumps join 3. There is always one more number than jumps.

board.text: Odd numbers from 1 to 51: how many?

beats.say: From 1 to 51, how many of the numbers are odd? Let's count them without writing every one.

ask.ifNot: 1 itself is odd, and it is inside the range, so it counts. Our list starts right at 1.

beats.say: Where does our list start? Which is the first odd number in the range?
So we start at 1. And the last one is 51 itself, because 51 is odd.
Odd numbers go up in jumps of 2: 1, 3, 5 and so on, all the way to 51.
From 1 to 51 is 50. Each jump is 2, so that is 25 jumps.

ask.ifNot: Think of fence posts. 1 jump joins 2 numbers, and 2 jumps join 3. There is always one more number than jumps.

beats.say: 25 jumps. So how many numbers are on our list?
One more than the jumps: 25 plus 1 is 26. That extra 1 is our starting number.
Check another way. Any 10 numbers in a row hold 5 odd ones. From 1 up to 51 there are 5 runs of 10, plus 51 itself, which is odd. That gives 26 again.
So there are 26 odd numbers from 1 to 51.
First one, last one, count the jumps of 2, and add 1. The add 1 is the step people forget.

board.text: Sum of the first 7 odd numbers = ?

beats.say: The first 7 odd numbers, all added together. Before the big sum, let's try some tiny ones and watch what happens.
The first odd number on its own is 1. The first 2 odd numbers, 1 plus 3, make 4. And 4 is 2 times 2.
The first 3 odd numbers: 1 plus 3 plus 5 makes 9. That is 3 times 3. Interesting!

ask.ifNot: Add them up: 1, 3, 5 and 7. Then compare with 4 times 4. They match.

beats.say: So what do you think the first 4 odd numbers, 1, 3, 5 and 7, add up to?
Yes, 4 times 4. Look at the picture: each new odd number wraps round the square like a letter L, and makes the next bigger square.
So the first 7 odd numbers must add up to 7 times 7.
And 7 times 7 is 49.
Check with pairs. The last odd number is 13. First plus last, 1 plus 13, is 14. Forwards and backwards gives 7 columns of 14, and half of that is 49.
So the sum of the first 7 odd numbers is 49.
So, count how many odd numbers there are, and multiply that count by itself. Isn't that neat?

board.text: Sum of the first 14 natural numbers = ?

beats.say: We need to add up the first 14 natural numbers. That is a long sum, so let's find a clever way.
Natural numbers are the counting numbers: 1, 2, 3 and so on. The first 14 of them end at 14.
Do not start adding from the left. Join the two ends instead: 1 plus 14 makes 15.

ask.ifNot: 2 plus 13 is 15 again. One number went up by 1 and the other came down by 1, so the total did not change.

beats.say: Now the second and the second last: 2 and 13. What do they make?
Yes, 15 again. Every pair, working inwards from the two ends, makes 15.
14 numbers make 7 pairs, because each pair uses up 2 numbers.
7 pairs of 15: 7 times 15 is 105.
Check another way. Write the list twice, once forwards and once backwards. That makes 14 columns of 15, and half of that is 105.
So the sum of the first 14 natural numbers is 105.
Whenever numbers go up in equal steps, pair the first with the last. Every pair gives the same total.

board.text: From 50 to 250: how many are divisible by 5?

beats.say: From 50 to 250, some numbers can be divided by 5 exactly. Our job is to count them.
Divisible by 5 means the number is in the 5 times table. So really, we are counting multiples of 5.

ask.ifNot: 250 itself is in the 5 times table, and it is inside our range. So 250 is the last one.

beats.say: Let's find the far end first. Which is the last multiple of 5 that does not go past 250?
5 times 50 is exactly 250. It lands right on the end of our range, so it counts.
Look at the 5 times table from its very start. 250 is multiple number 50. So up to 250 there are 50 multiples of 5.
Careful here: 50 itself is in the 5 times table, so it counts. The ones that are too small stop at 45, which is 5 times 9.

ask.ifNot: The too small ones run up to 45, and 45 is 5 times 9. So exactly 9 of them go.

beats.say: So out of the 50 multiples, how many are too small and have to go?
So we take 9 away from 50, and 41 are left.
Check another way. From 50 to 250 is 200. That is 40 jumps of 5, and 40 jumps join 41 numbers.
So 41 numbers from 50 to 250 are divisible by 5.
So, count the multiples up to the top end, then remove the ones below the bottom end. No long lists needed.

board.text: Sum of the first 17 even numbers = ?

beats.say: We need to add up the first 17 even numbers. That is a long sum, so let's find a clever way.
Even numbers go 2, 4, 6 and so on. Each one is 2 times its position in the list, so the last one is 2 times 17, which is 34.
Here is the trick. Add the first and the last: 2 plus 34 makes 36.

ask.ifNot: 4 plus 32 is 36 again. One number went up by 2 and the other came down by 2, so the total did not change.

beats.say: Now the second and the second last: 4 and 32. What do they make?
36 once more. Keep stepping inwards from both ends, and every pair makes 36.
17 is an odd count, so one number is left alone in the middle. It is half of 36, which is 18. The rest make 8 pairs.
8 pairs of 36, plus the middle 18, makes 306.
Check another way. Write the list twice, once forwards and once backwards. That makes 17 columns of 36, and half of that is 306.
So the sum of the first 17 even numbers is 306.
Pair the ends, count the pairs, multiply. That trick turns a long sum into a short one.

board.text: Even numbers from 20 to 50: how many?

So we start at 20. And the last one is 50 itself, because 50 is even.
Even numbers go up in jumps of 2: 20, 22, 24 and so on, all the way to 50.
From 20 to 50 is 30. Each jump is 2, so that is 15 jumps.

ask.ifNot: Think of fence posts. 1 jump joins 2 numbers, and 2 jumps join 3. There is always one more number than jumps.

board.text: From 50 to 250: how many are divisible by 8?

Divisible by 8 means the number is in the 8 times table. So really, we are counting multiples of 8.

beats.say: Let's find the far end first. Which is the last multiple of 8 that does not go past 250?
8 times 31 is 248. One more step gives 256, and that is past 250.
Look at the 8 times table from its very start. 248 is multiple number 31. So up to 250 there are 31 multiples of 8.
But our range only starts at 50. 8 times 6 is 48, still too small. The next one, 56, is the first one inside.

ask.ifNot: The too small ones run up to 48, and 48 is 8 times 6. So exactly 6 of them go.

beats.say: So out of the 31 multiples, how many are too small and have to go?
31 take away 6 leaves 25.
Check another way. From 56 to 248 is 192. That is 24 jumps of 8, and 24 jumps join 25 numbers.
So 25 numbers from 50 to 250 are divisible by 8.
So, count the multiples up to the top end, then remove the ones below the bottom end. No long lists needed.

board.text: Even numbers from 10 to 40: how many?

beats.say: We want to know how many even numbers there are from 10 to 40. Both ends count, if they are even.

ask.ifNot: 10 itself is even, and it is inside the range, so it counts. Our list starts right at 10.

beats.say: Where does our list start? Which is the first even number in the range?
So we start at 10. And the last one is 40 itself, because 40 is even.
Even numbers go up in jumps of 2: 10, 12, 14 and so on, all the way to 40.
From 10 to 40 is 30. Each jump is 2, so that is 15 jumps.

ask.ifNot: Think of fence posts. 1 jump joins 2 numbers, and 2 jumps join 3. There is always one more number than jumps.

beats.say: 15 jumps. So how many numbers are on our list?
One more than the jumps: 15 plus 1 is 16. That extra 1 is our starting number.
Check another way. Any 10 numbers in a row hold 5 even ones. From 10 up to 40 there are 3 runs of 10, plus 40 itself, which is even. That gives 16 again.
So there are 16 even numbers from 10 to 40.
First one, last one, count the jumps of 2, and add 1. The add 1 is the step people forget.

board.text: From 100 to 300: how many are divisible by 7?

beats.say: We are counting the numbers from 100 to 300 that 7 divides exactly, with nothing left over.
Divisible by 7 means the number is in the 7 times table. So really, we are counting multiples of 7.

ask.ifNot: 301 is past 300, and 287 is not the last one we can reach. The last multiple of 7 inside the range is 294.

beats.say: Let's find the far end first. Which is the last multiple of 7 that does not go past 300?
7 times 42 is 294. One more step gives 301, and that is past 300.
Look at the 7 times table from its very start. 294 is multiple number 42. So up to 300 there are 42 multiples of 7.
But our range only starts at 100. 7 times 14 is 98, still too small. The next one, 105, is the first one inside.

ask.ifNot: The too small ones run up to 98, and 98 is 7 times 14. So exactly 14 of them go.

beats.say: So out of the 42 multiples, how many are too small and have to go?
42 take away 14 leaves 28.

board.text: Triangle: base 20 cm, height 7 cm. Area = ?

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: Here is our triangle. Its base is 20 centimetres and its height is 7 centimetres. We want its area, the flat space inside.

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides is for the walk round the edge. The space inside a rectangle is its length times its breadth.

beats.say: Counting squares inside a triangle is awkward. So let me box it in: a rectangle around the triangle, with the same base and the same height. How do we find the area of that rectangle?
The area of a rectangle is its length times its breadth. Here that means base times height.
20 times 7 is 140.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing once more. The triangle covers only half of the dashed rectangle. So we need half of 140.

beats.say: Now look closely. The two corner pieces outside the triangle fit together to make another triangle, just the same size. So what do we do with 140?
So the rule for a triangle is: half of base times height.
Half of 140 is 70. And see how it is written: a half, times 20, times 7.

spec.note: Area = 70 sq. cm

beats.say: So the area of the triangle is 70 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area counts little squares.
A quick check: two triangles of 70 make 140, the whole rectangle. It fits.
The method in one line: half of base times height. If you stop at base times height, you have found the whole rectangle, not the triangle.

spec.note: Circumference = ?

beats.say: Here is our circle. Its radius, from the centre out to the edge, is 14 centimetres. We want the circumference, and we are told to use 22 over 7 for pi.
Circumference is the walk all the way round the circle. And here is a lovely fact: for every circle, that walk is a little more than 3 times the distance straight across. That number is pi.

ask.ifNot: The radius only goes from the centre to the edge. The diameter goes right across, through the centre. That is 2 radii, so 2 times 14.

beats.say: We were given the radius, 14. So what is the distance straight across, the diameter?
The diameter is 2 radii: 2 times 14 is 28 centimetres. That is why the rule is often written as 2 times pi times the radius.
Now we need 22 over 7, times 28. Divide by the 7 first, because 28 is in the 7 times table: 28 divided by 7 is 4.
Then multiply by the 22. 22 times 4 is 88.

spec.note: Circumference = 88 cm

beats.say: So the circumference is 88 centimetres. Plain centimetres, because it is a length, a walk round the edge.
Does that make sense? 3 times 28 is 84, and our answer, 88, is a little more than that. Just as pi promised.
So: circumference is 2 times pi times the radius. The slip to watch for is forgetting to double the radius, which gives only half the walk.

board.text: Rectangle: length 25 cm, breadth 5 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Look at this rectangle. The length is 25 centimetres and the breadth is 5 centimetres. How far is it all the way round?
Perimeter is a walk all the way round the edge, back to where you started. Opposite sides of a rectangle are equal, so there are 2 lengths and 2 breadths. Let me label all 4 sides.

ask.ifNot: 25 plus 5 only gets us halfway, along one length and one breadth. The walk goes along all 4 sides. And 25 times 5 would be the space inside, the area.

beats.say: Which sum takes us all the way round?
Let's walk it. One length and one breadth: 25 plus 5 is 30. That is halfway round.
The other two sides are the same again, so we double it: 30 plus 30 is 60.
That is where the rule comes from: add the length and the breadth, then double.

spec.note: Perimeter = 60 cm

beats.say: So the perimeter is 60 centimetres. Plain centimetres, because a perimeter is a length.
Check with the whole walk: 25 plus 5 plus 25 plus 5 makes 60.
The method in one line: perimeter is 2 times, length plus breadth. Do not stop after adding just two sides.
Here is 43 degrees, drawn on a straight line. Its supplementary angle is the other piece of that line, the one marked with a question mark.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles lie along a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That makes 180 degrees. 90 is for a corner, a right angle.

beats.say: Stand at the point and turn from one end of the line to the other. That is a half turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. So 43 degrees, plus our missing angle, makes 180 degrees.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 180 take away 43.

beats.say: We know the whole, 180, and one part, 43. How do we find the other part?
Let's take 43 away in two easy hops. First the 40: 180 take away 40 leaves 140.
Now the 3 that is left: 140 take away 3 leaves 137. So 180 minus 43 is 137.
So the supplementary angle is 137 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 43 plus 137 makes 180. It fits exactly.
So for a supplementary angle, take the angle away from 180. To remember which is which: S for supplementary, S for straight line. C for complementary, C for corner.
Here is our triangle. Two of its angles are 41 degrees and 71 degrees. The third one, at the top, is our mystery.

ask.ifNot: A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. So the 3 angles of a triangle always make 180 degrees.

beats.say: Here is something you can try with paper. Tear the 3 corners off any triangle and put them side by side. They always make a straight line. So how much do the 3 angles make together?

board.text: Angles of a triangle add up to 180°

beats.say: A straight line is a half turn, 180 degrees. So the 3 angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees.
First, how much have the two angles we know used up? 41 plus 71 is 112.

ask.ifNot: Both known angles have to come off the 180, not just one of them. Together they are 112, so it is 180 take away 112.

beats.say: So 112 of the 180 degrees is gone. What sum finds the third angle?
Let's take 112 away in two easy hops. First the 110: 180 take away 110 leaves 70.
Now the 2 that is left: 70 take away 2 leaves 68. So 180 minus 112 is 68.
So the third angle is 68 degrees. Into the drawing it goes.
Check: 41 plus 71 plus 68 makes 180. All three together make the straight line.
So for any triangle: add the two angles you know, then take the total away from 180. The slip to watch for is taking away only one of them.

board.text: On a straight line: x° and 116°. x = ?

beats.say: Here is a straight line with two angles sitting on it. One is 116 degrees. The other is called x, and we want to know its size.

ask.ifNot: The two angles lie along a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That makes 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

beats.say: Stand where the two angles meet. Facing along the line one way, then turning to face the other way, is a half turn. So how much do the two angles make together?
A half turn is 180 degrees. So x, plus 116, equals 180. Now it is an equation.

ask.ifNot: To undo plus 116, we take away 116. And to keep the two sides level, we take it from both sides.

beats.say: We want x on its own. What do we do about the plus 116?
To undo plus 116, we take 116 away, from both sides.
Let's take 116 away in two easy hops. First the 110: 180 take away 110 leaves 70.
Now the 6 that is left: 70 take away 6 leaves 64. So 180 minus 116 is 64.
So x equals 64. The other angle is 64 degrees.
Check: 64 plus 116 makes 180, a full straight line. It fits.
So angles on a straight line always make 180 degrees. Take the one you know away from 180, and you have the other.

board.text: Lines cross: one angle is 108°. Opposite angle = ?

beats.say: Two straight lines cross and make 4 angles. One of them is 108 degrees. We want the angle vertically opposite: the one straight across the crossing point.
I have called the two angles next door p and q. Now, here is what we know about a straight line: it is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees.
Look at 108 degrees and its neighbour, p. They sit side by side on one straight line. Let's take 108 away in two easy hops. First the 100: 180 take away 100 leaves 80.
Now the 8 that is left: 80 take away 8 leaves 72. So 180 minus 108 is 72.

ask.ifNot: p and the mystery angle share a straight line, so together they make 180 degrees. We take p, which is 72, away from 180.

beats.say: So p is 72 degrees. Now look at p and our mystery angle. They sit side by side on the other straight line. So what is the mystery angle?
Let's take 72 away in two easy hops. First the 70: 180 take away 70 leaves 110.
Now the 2 that is left: 110 take away 2 leaves 108. So 180 minus 72 is 108.
108 degrees. Exactly the angle we started with! That always happens: angles straight across from each other are equal.
So next time you can say it straight away: the vertically opposite angle is equal, 108 degrees. The slip to watch for is giving 72, which is the neighbour on the line.

Careful here: 100 itself is in the 4 times table, so it counts. The ones that are too small stop at 96, which is 4 times 24.

beats.say: So out of the 75 multiples, how many are too small and have to go?

board.text: Odd numbers from 100 to 130: how many?

Odd numbers go up in jumps of 2: 101, 103, 105 and so on, all the way to 129.
From 101 to 129 is 28. Each jump is 2, so that is 14 jumps.

ask.ifNot: Think of fence posts. 1 jump joins 2 numbers, and 2 jumps join 3. There is always one more number than jumps.

beats.say: 14 jumps. So how many numbers are on our list?
14 jumps join 15 numbers. The extra 1 is the number we started on.
Check another way. Any 10 numbers in a row hold 5 odd ones. From 100 up to 130 there are 3 runs of 10. The 130 left at the end is even, so it adds nothing. 15 again.
So there are 15 odd numbers from 100 to 130.
Find the two ends, count the jumps between them, then add 1 for the starting number. That works every time.

board.text: Even numbers from 100 to 120: how many?

beats.say: From 100 to 120, how many of the numbers are even? Let's count them without writing every one.

ask.ifNot: 100 itself is even, and it is inside the range, so it counts. Our list starts right at 100.

beats.say: Where does our list start? Which is the first even number in the range?
So we start at 100. And the last one is 120 itself, because 120 is even.
Even numbers go up in jumps of 2: 100, 102, 104 and so on, all the way to 120.
From 100 to 120 is 20. Each jump is 2, so that is 10 jumps.

ask.ifNot: Think of fence posts. 1 jump joins 2 numbers, and 2 jumps join 3. There is always one more number than jumps.

beats.say: 10 jumps. So how many numbers are on our list?
10 jumps join 11 numbers. The extra 1 is the number we started on.
Check another way. Any 10 numbers in a row hold 5 even ones. From 100 up to 120 there are 2 runs of 10, plus 120 itself, which is even. That gives 11 again.
So there are 11 even numbers from 100 to 120.
Find the two ends, count the jumps between them, then add 1 for the starting number. That works every time.

board.text: From 10 to 60: how many are divisible by 3?

beats.say: From 10 to 60, some numbers can be divided by 3 exactly. Our job is to count them.
Divisible by 3 means the number is in the 3 times table. So really, we are counting multiples of 3.

ask.ifNot: 60 itself is in the 3 times table, and it is inside our range. So 60 is the last one.

beats.say: Start at the top end. What is the biggest multiple of 3 that is not more than 60?
3 times 20 is exactly 60. It lands right on the end of our range, so it counts.
Look at the 3 times table from its very start. 60 is multiple number 20. So up to 60 there are 20 multiples of 3.
But our range only starts at 10. 3 times 3 is 9, still too small. The next one, 12, is the first one inside.

ask.ifNot: The too small ones run up to 9, and 9 is 3 times 3. So exactly 3 of them go.

beats.say: So out of the 20 multiples, how many are too small and have to go?
20 take away 3 leaves 17.
Check another way. From 12 to 60 is 48. That is 16 jumps of 3, and 16 jumps join 17 numbers.
So 17 numbers from 10 to 60 are divisible by 3.
The plan: find the last multiple, count from the start of the table, then take away the ones that are too small.

board.text: Odd numbers from 50 to 70: how many?

beats.say: We want to know how many odd numbers there are from 50 to 70. Both ends count, if they are odd.

ask.ifNot: 50 is even, so it does not count. The very next number, 51, is the first odd one.

beats.say: Where does our list start? Which is the first odd number in the range?
So we start at 51. And the last one is 69, because 70 is even.
Odd numbers go up in jumps of 2: 51, 53, 55 and so on, all the way to 69.
From 51 to 69 is 18. Each jump is 2, so that is 9 jumps.

ask.ifNot: Think of fence posts. 1 jump joins 2 numbers, and 2 jumps join 3. There is always one more number than jumps.

beats.say: 9 jumps. So how many numbers are on our list?
One more than the jumps: 9 plus 1 is 10. That extra 1 is our starting number.
Check another way. Any 10 numbers in a row hold 5 odd ones. From 50 up to 70 there are 2 runs of 10. The 70 left at the end is even, so it adds nothing. 10 again.
So there are 10 odd numbers from 50 to 70.
First one, last one, count the jumps of 2, and add 1. The add 1 is the step people forget.

board.text: Sum of the first 20 odd numbers = ?

beats.say: Add up the first 20 odd numbers: 1, 3, 5 and so on. Let's start small and hunt for a pattern.
The first odd number on its own is 1. The first 2 odd numbers, 1 plus 3, make 4. And 4 is 2 times 2.
The first 3 odd numbers: 1 plus 3 plus 5 makes 9. That is 3 times 3. Interesting!

ask.ifNot: Add them up: 1, 3, 5 and 7. Then compare with 4 times 4. They match.

beats.say: So what do you think the first 4 odd numbers, 1, 3, 5 and 7, add up to?
Yes, 4 times 4. Look at the picture: each new odd number wraps round the square like a letter L, and makes the next bigger square.
So the first 20 odd numbers must add up to 20 times 20.
20 times 20 is 400.
Check with pairs. The last odd number is 39. First plus last, 1 plus 39, is 40. Forwards and backwards gives 20 columns of 40, and half of that is 400.
So the sum of the first 20 odd numbers is 400.
So, count how many odd numbers there are, and multiply that count by itself. Isn't that neat?
Look at this. 6 x, plus 9, plus 8 x, minus 5. Four pieces, and some of them can be joined together. Let's see which.
Think of x as a box with a secret number of sweets inside. 6 x is 6 boxes, and 8 x is 8 more boxes. The plain numbers are loose sweets. What can we count together?

choices: a box and some loose sweets
ask.ifNot: Boxes go with boxes, and loose sweets go with loose sweets. We cannot add a box to a loose sweet, because we do not know how many are inside the box.

beats.say: So gather the x terms. 6 x and 8 x together make 14 x.
Now the plain numbers. Careful: the sign in front of a number belongs to that number. So this is 9 minus 5, which is 4.
So we have 14 x and 4. Here is where people slip. Can we squash those two into one term?

choices: No, they are not like terms
ask.ifNot: 14 x means 14 lots of a hidden number. 4 is a plain number. They are different families, so they stay side by side.

beats.say: That leaves 14 x plus 4. It cannot get any shorter than that.
Let's test it with a number. Say x is 1. The long one is 6 plus 9 plus 8 minus 5, which is 18. The short one is 14 plus 4, also 18. They match.
The plan every time: x terms with x terms, numbers with numbers, and each sign stays with its own term.
Two letters this time. x is 5 and y is 1. Our job is to find the value of 5 x plus 1 y.
First, what does 5 x turn into when x is 5?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 5 x means 5 times x, and here that is 5 times 5.

beats.say: So we swap each letter for its number. 5 x becomes 5 times 5, and 1 y becomes 1 times 1.
Now we have two multiplications and one addition. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying comes before adding. So we work out each times first, and only then add the two answers.

beats.say: 5 times 5 is 25. And 1 y is just one single y, so that is 1.
Now add them. 25 plus 1 is 26. So 5 x plus 1 y is worth 26.
So for any question like this: swap each letter for its number, do the times first, then add. And 5 x is 5 times x, never the two digits side by side.
This one is a recipe. Start with 8, multiply it by 2, then add 9. We just have to follow it in the right order.
Which step comes first?

ask.ifNot: Read the recipe again: multiply it by 2 comes before add 9. So first we work out 8 times 2.

beats.say: So we multiply. 8 times 2 makes 16.
Next the recipe says add 9. What do we add it to?

ask.ifNot: We add it to the number we are holding now, not the one we started with. Right now we are holding 16.

beats.say: 16 plus 9 is 25. That is what we get.
Here is the clever bit. If we call the starting number n, the whole recipe is 2 n plus 9. That is all algebra is: a recipe, with a letter standing for the number.
Put 8 in for n. 2 times 8, plus 9, is 25. The same answer. Just never add the 2 and the 9 first, because that changes the recipe.
So: follow the steps in the order they are given, one at a time, and always carry on from the number you have reached.

Before we swap anything: when x is 6, what is 3 x?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 3 x means 3 times x, and here that is 3 times 6.

ask.ifNot: Multiplying always goes before adding and taking away. So 3 times 6 comes first.

beats.say: 3 times 6 is 18. So now we have 18, plus 13, minus 5.
Now we go left to right. 18 plus 13 is 31. Then 31 minus 5 is 26.
That gives 26. Remember the order: number in for the letter, then the times, then the plus and minus from left to right.

beats.say: So the short form is 11 x plus 14. Same value, far fewer pieces.
Let's test it with a number. Say x is 2. The long one comes to 36. The short one, 11 times 2 plus 14, comes to 36 as well. They match.

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 8 x means 8 times x, and here that is 8 times 6.

Neha buys 4 pens at 10 rupees each, and hands over 50 rupees. We want the change that comes back.

board.text: 4 pens at Rs.10 each. Pays Rs.50.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 50 rupees pays for the pens, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the pens
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 4 pens, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 4 pens at 10 rupees each: that is 4 times 10. 4 times 10 is 40.
Careful: 40 is only the cost, not the answer. Neha paid 50. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 40 away from 50.

beats.say: Count up from 40 to 50. That is 10 more.
So Neha gets 10 rupees back.
Check it the shopkeeper's way. The cost, 40, plus the change, 10, should make the 50 that was paid. It does.
So a change sum takes two moves. First find the total cost. Then take it away from the money paid. Your turn next!
The bag costs Nikhil 100 rupees: that is the cost price. Then it is sold at a profit of 15 per cent. What is the selling price?
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 100 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
A profit means it is sold for more than it cost, so the bottom bar is longer. That extra bit on the end is the profit.
The profit is 15 per cent. But 15 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 100 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
And here the cost price is exactly 100 rupees. So 15 out of every 100 is simply 15 rupees. That is the profit.
So the profit is 15 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 100 plus 15 is 115. So the selling price is 115 rupees.
Does that make sense? A profit should lift the selling price above the cost price, and 115 is 15 more than 100. It fits.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. You can do the next one yourself!
Riya pays 300 rupees for a laptop. That is the cost price. It is sold at a loss of 15 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 300 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
With a loss, the selling price is smaller than the cost price. So the bottom bar stops short, and the gap is the loss.
The loss is 15 per cent. But 15 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 300 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the classic trap. Loss per cent is always worked out on the cost price, never on the selling price. And per cent means out of every 100.
First find 10 per cent. That is one tenth, so divide by 10. 300 divided by 10 gives 30.
5 per cent is half of 10 per cent. Half of 30 is 15.
15 per cent is 10 per cent and 5 per cent together. 30 plus 15 makes 45. That is the loss.
So the loss is 45 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 300 take away 45 is 255. So the selling price is 255 rupees.
Quick check. With a loss, the selling price must be smaller than the cost price. 255 is 45 below 300. Good.
So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. Now you try one!
8 sharpeners cost 24 rupees altogether. We want the cost of just one sharpener.
Picture the 24 rupees as one long bar, cut into 8 equal pieces, one piece for each sharpener. Every sharpener costs the same.
So which sum finds the cost of one sharpener?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 24 rupees equally among 8 sharpeners. Sharing equally is dividing.

beats.say: Think of the 8 times table. 8 times what makes 24? 8 times 3 is 24.
There it is: each sharpener costs 3 rupees.
Check by building it back up. 8 sharpeners at 3 rupees each: 8 times 3 is 24. It fits.
So when you know the cost of many and want the cost of one, divide the total by how many. You can do the next one yourself!
Here is a long expression. 2 x, plus 10, plus 7 x, plus 10. Simplify means write it shorter, without changing what it is worth.
Some of these pieces belong together. The ones with an x are one family, and the plain numbers are another. Which two are like terms?

ask.ifNot: Like terms have the same letter part. 2 x and 7 x both have an x, so they are family. 10 has no x at all.

beats.say: So gather the x terms. 2 x and 7 x together make 9 x.
Now the plain numbers. 10 plus 10 makes 20.
So we have 9 x and 20. Here is where people slip. Can we squash those two into one term?

ask.ifNot: 9 x means 9 lots of a hidden number. 20 is a plain number. They are different families, so they stay side by side.

beats.say: First the x family. 8 lots of x and 4 more lots of x make 12 lots of x.
Now the plain numbers. 3 plus 4 makes 7.
So we have 12 x and 7. Here is where people slip. Can we squash those two into one term?

choices: No, they are not like terms
ask.ifNot: 12 x means 12 lots of a hidden number. 7 is a plain number. They are different families, so they stay side by side.

beats.say: That leaves 12 x plus 7. It cannot get any shorter than that.
Let's test it with a number. Say x is 1. The long one is 8 plus 3 plus 4 plus 4, which is 19. The short one is 12 plus 7, also 19. They match.
So to simplify: gather the x terms, gather the plain numbers, and keep the two families apart.
We are told that x is 2 and y is 3. And we want to know what 4 x plus 4 y is worth.
First, what does 4 x turn into when x is 2?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 4 x means 4 times x, and here that is 4 times 2.

beats.say: So we swap each letter for its number. 4 x becomes 4 times 2, and 4 y becomes 4 times 3.
Now we have two multiplications and one addition. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying comes before adding. So we work out each times first, and only then add the two answers.

beats.say: 4 times 2 is 8. And 4 times 3 is 12.
Now add them. 8 plus 12 is 20. So 4 x plus 4 y is worth 20.
The plan: put the numbers in place of the letters, multiply, then add. A number next to a letter always means times.
A number game! Our number is 10. We multiply it by 5, and then we add 11. Let's take it one step at a time.
Which step comes first?

ask.ifNot: Read the recipe again: multiply it by 5 comes before add 11. So first we work out 10 times 5.

beats.say: 10 times 5 is 50.
Next the recipe says add 11. What do we add it to?

ask.ifNot: We add it to the number we are holding now, not the one we started with. Right now we are holding 50.

beats.say: 50 plus 11 is 61. That is what we get.
Here is the clever bit. If we call the starting number n, the whole recipe is 5 n plus 11. That is all algebra is: a recipe, with a letter standing for the number.
Put 10 in for n. 5 times 10, plus 11, is 61. The same answer. Just never add the 5 and the 11 first, because that changes the recipe.
So: follow the steps in the order they are given, one at a time, and always carry on from the number you have reached.
This time the hidden number is not hidden at all: x is 7. So we can work out what 2 x, plus 2, minus 3 is worth.
Before we swap anything: when x is 7, what is 2 x?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 2 x means 2 times x, and here that is 2 times 7.

beats.say: So we rub out the x and write 7 in its place, with a times sign. 2 times 7, plus 2, minus 3.
Three jobs here: a times, a plus and a minus. Which one goes first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying always goes before adding and taking away. So 2 times 7 comes first.

beats.say: 2 times 7 is 14. So now we have 14, plus 2, minus 3.
Now we go left to right. 14 plus 2 is 16. Then 16 minus 3 is 13.
That gives 13. Remember the order: number in for the letter, then the times, then the plus and minus from left to right.
2 x, plus 10, plus 2 x, minus 5. That is quite a mouthful. Let's tidy it up, so it says the same thing in fewer pieces.

ask.ifNot: We add it to the number we are holding now, not the one we started with. Right now we are holding 45.

Here is the clever bit. If we call the starting number n, the whole recipe is 3 n plus 15. That is all algebra is: a recipe, with a letter standing for the number.
Put 15 in for n. 3 times 15, plus 15, is 60. The same answer. Just never add the 3 and the 15 first, because that changes the recipe.
So: follow the steps in the order they are given, one at a time, and always carry on from the number you have reached.
We know that x is 5. We want the value of 6 x, plus 1, minus 7.
Before we swap anything: when x is 5, what is 6 x?

Now we go left to right. 30 plus 1 is 31. Then 31 minus 7 is 24.
So when x is 5, the whole thing is worth 24. The plan: swap the letter for its number, multiply first, then work left to right.

beats.say: So gather the x terms. 6 x and 2 x together make 8 x.
Now the plain numbers. 5 plus 5 makes 10.

ask.ifNot: 8 x means 8 lots of a hidden number. 10 is a plain number. They are different families, so they stay side by side.

beats.say: So the short form is 8 x plus 10. Same value, far fewer pieces.
Let's test it with a number. Say x is 1. The long one is 6 plus 5 plus 2 plus 5, which is 18. The short one is 8 plus 10, also 18. They match.
The plan every time: x terms with x terms, numbers with numbers, and each sign stays with its own term.
We are told that x is 3 and y is 3. And we want to know what 5 x plus 2 y is worth.
First, what does 5 x turn into when x is 3?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 5 x means 5 times x, and here that is 5 times 3.

beats.say: So we swap each letter for its number. 5 x becomes 5 times 3, and 2 y becomes 2 times 3.
Now we have two multiplications and one addition. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying comes before adding. So we work out each times first, and only then add the two answers.

beats.say: 5 times 3 is 15. And 2 times 3 is 6.
Now add them. 15 plus 6 is 21. So 5 x plus 2 y is worth 21.
The plan: put the numbers in place of the letters, multiply, then add. A number next to a letter always means times.
A number game! Our number is 7. We multiply it by 4, and then we add 5. Let's take it one step at a time.
Which step comes first?

ask.ifNot: Read the recipe again: multiply it by 4 comes before add 5. So first we work out 7 times 4.

beats.say: 7 times 4 is 28.
Next the recipe says add 5. What do we add it to?

ask.ifNot: We add it to the number we are holding now, not the one we started with. Right now we are holding 28.

beats.say: 28 plus 5 is 33. That is what we get.
Here is the clever bit. If we call the starting number n, the whole recipe is 4 n plus 5. That is all algebra is: a recipe, with a letter standing for the number.
Put 7 in for n. 4 times 7, plus 5, is 33. The same answer. Just never add the 4 and the 5 first, because that changes the recipe.
The plan for any number recipe: do the first step, keep the result, then do the next step to that result.
This time the hidden number is not hidden at all: x is 5. So we can work out what 4 x, plus 2, minus 6 is worth.
Before we swap anything: when x is 5, what is 4 x?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 4 x means 4 times x, and here that is 4 times 5.

beats.say: So we rub out the x and write 5 in its place, with a times sign. 4 times 5, plus 2, minus 6.
Three jobs here: a times, a plus and a minus. Which one goes first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying always goes before adding and taking away. So 4 times 5 comes first.

beats.say: 4 times 5 is 20. So now we have 20, plus 2, minus 6.
Now we go left to right. 20 plus 2 is 22. Then 22 minus 6 is 16.
So when x is 5, the whole thing is worth 16. The plan: swap the letter for its number, multiply first, then work left to right.
Look at this. 12 x, plus 9, plus 2 x, minus 7. Four pieces, and some of them can be joined together. Let's see which.
Think of x as a box with a secret number of sweets inside. 12 x is 12 boxes, and 2 x is 2 more boxes. The plain numbers are loose sweets. What can we count together?

choices: a box and some loose sweets
ask.ifNot: Boxes go with boxes, and loose sweets go with loose sweets. We cannot add a box to a loose sweet, because we do not know how many are inside the box.

beats.say: So gather the x terms. 12 x and 2 x together make 14 x.
Now the plain numbers. Careful: the sign in front of a number belongs to that number. So this is 9 minus 7, which is 2.
So we have 14 x and 2. Here is where people slip. Can we squash those two into one term?

choices: No, they are not like terms
ask.ifNot: 14 x means 14 lots of a hidden number. 2 is a plain number. They are different families, so they stay side by side.

beats.say: That leaves 14 x plus 2. It cannot get any shorter than that.
Let's test it with a number. Say x is 2. The long one comes to 30. The short one, 14 times 2 plus 2, comes to 30 as well. They match.
The plan every time: x terms with x terms, numbers with numbers, and each sign stays with its own term.
Two letters this time. x is 5 and y is 4. Our job is to find the value of 4 x plus 4 y.
Before we swap anything: when x is 5, what is 4 x?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 4 x means 4 times x, and here that is 4 times 5.

beats.say: So we swap each letter for its number. 4 x becomes 4 times 5, and 4 y becomes 4 times 4.
Now we have two multiplications and one addition. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying comes before adding. So we work out each times first, and only then add the two answers.

beats.say: 4 times 5 is 20. And 4 times 4 is 16.
Now add them. 20 plus 16 is 36. So 4 x plus 4 y is worth 36.
So for any question like this: swap each letter for its number, do the times first, then add. And 4 x is 4 times x, never the two digits side by side.
This one is a recipe. Start with 20, multiply it by 5, then add 10. We just have to follow it in the right order.
What do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: Read the recipe again: multiply it by 5 comes before add 10. So first we work out 20 times 5.

beats.say: So we multiply. 20 times 5 makes 100.
Next the recipe says add 10. What do we add it to?

ask.ifNot: We add it to the number we are holding now, not the one we started with. Right now we are holding 100.

beats.say: 100 plus 10 is 110. That is what we get.
Here is the clever bit. If we call the starting number n, the whole recipe is 5 n plus 10. That is all algebra is: a recipe, with a letter standing for the number.
Put 20 in for n. 5 times 20, plus 10, is 110. The same answer. Just never add the 5 and the 10 first, because that changes the recipe.
So: follow the steps in the order they are given, one at a time, and always carry on from the number you have reached.
We know that x is 3. We want the value of 4 x, plus 14, minus 8.
Before we swap anything: when x is 3, what is 4 x?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 4 x means 4 times x, and here that is 4 times 3.

beats.say: So we rub out the x and write 3 in its place, with a times sign. 4 times 3, plus 14, minus 8.
Three jobs here: a times, a plus and a minus. Which one goes first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying always goes before adding and taking away. So 4 times 3 comes first.

beats.say: 4 times 3 is 12. So now we have 12, plus 14, minus 8.
Now we go left to right. 12 plus 14 is 26. Then 26 minus 8 is 18.
That gives 18. Remember the order: number in for the letter, then the times, then the plus and minus from left to right.
Here is a shop sum with two parts. 8 erasers at 6 rupees each, and Vivek pays with 63 rupees. How much change?

board.text: 8 erasers at Rs.6 each. Pays Rs.63.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 63 rupees pays for the erasers, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the erasers
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 8 erasers, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 8 erasers at 6 rupees each: that is 8 times 6. 8 times 6 is 48.
Careful: 48 is only the cost, not the answer. Vivek paid 63. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 48 away from 63.

beats.say: From 63, take off the 48. That leaves 15.
So Vivek gets 15 rupees back.
Check it the shopkeeper's way. The cost, 48, plus the change, 15, should make the 63 that was paid. It does.
So a change sum takes two moves. First find the total cost. Then take it away from the money paid. You can do the next one yourself!
The book costs Isha 50 rupees: that is the cost price. Then it is sold at a profit of 20 per cent. What is the selling price?
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 50 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
With a profit, the selling price is bigger than the cost price. So the bottom bar sticks out, and the bit that sticks out is the profit.
The profit is 20 per cent. But 20 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 50 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
Start with the friendly one, 10 per cent. 10 per cent is one tenth, so we divide by 10. 50 divided by 10 is 5.
Now, 20 per cent is just 10 per cent, 2 times over. 2 times 5 makes 10. That is the profit.
So the profit is 10 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 50 plus 10 is 60. So the selling price is 60 rupees.
Quick check. With a profit, the selling price must be bigger than the cost price. 60 is 10 above 50. Good.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. Your turn next!
Karan pays 200 rupees for a phone. That is the cost price. It is sold at a loss of 20 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 200 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
With a loss, the selling price is smaller than the cost price. So the bottom bar stops short, and the gap is the loss.
The loss is 20 per cent. But 20 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 200 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Loss per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
First find 10 per cent. That is one tenth, so divide by 10. 200 divided by 10 gives 20.
Now, 20 per cent is just 10 per cent, 2 times over. 2 times 20 makes 40. That is the loss.
So the loss is 40 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 200 take away 40 is 160. So the selling price is 160 rupees.
Does that make sense? A loss should drop the selling price below the cost price, and 160 is 40 less than 200. It fits.
So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. Your turn next!
12 pens cost 120 rupees altogether. We want the cost of just one pen.
Picture the 120 rupees as one long bar, cut into 12 equal pieces, one piece for each pen. Every pen costs the same.
So which sum finds the cost of one pen?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 120 rupees equally among 12 pens. Sharing equally is dividing.

beats.say: 120 is exactly 12 tens. So 120 divided by 12 is 10.
So one pen costs 10 rupees.
Check by building it back up. 12 pens at 10 rupees each: 12 times 10 is 120. It fits.
So when you know the cost of many and want the cost of one, divide the total by how many. Now you try one!

board.text: 10 rulers at Rs.10 each. Pays Rs.105.

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 100 away from 105.

beats.say: Count up from 100 to 105. That is 5 more.
So Siya gets 5 rupees back.
Check it the shopkeeper's way. The cost, 100, plus the change, 5, should make the 105 that was paid. It does.
So a change sum takes two moves. First find the total cost. Then take it away from the money paid. Your turn next!

The loss is 20 per cent. But 20 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 300 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Loss per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
10 per cent is the easy one: it is one tenth. 300 divided by 10 is 30.
20 per cent is 2 lots of 10 per cent. 2 times 30 is 60. That is the loss.
So the loss is 60 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 300 take away 60 is 240. So the selling price is 240 rupees.

20 books cost 240 rupees altogether. We want the cost of just one book.
Think of the 240 rupees as a bar shared into 20 equal pieces. Each piece is the price of one book.
So which sum finds the cost of one book?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 240 rupees equally among 20 books. Sharing equally is dividing.

beats.say: Dividing by 20 is easier in two steps: divide by 10, then by 2. First, 240 divided by 10 is 24.
Then 24 divided by 2 is 12. So 240 divided by 20 is 12.
So one book costs 12 rupees.
Check by building it back up. 20 books at 12 rupees each: 20 times 12 is 240. It fits.
So when you know the cost of many and want the cost of one, divide the total by how many. Your turn next!
Here is Arjun's shopping. 13 pens, at 5 rupees each. We want the total cost.
A shopkeeper would write a bill like this. The price of one pen, how many, and a space for the cost.
So which sum gives the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 13 pens costs 5 rupees. That is 5 rupees, 13 times over, so we multiply.

beats.say: We multiply, because it is the same price again and again. 13 is 10 and 3. So we do it in two easy bites. 10 times 5 is 50.
And 3 times 5 is 15.
Put the two bites together. 50 plus 15 makes 65. So 13 times 5 is 65.
So Arjun pays 65 rupees altogether.
Let us check by sharing it back out. 65 rupees, in lots of 5 rupees, gives 13 pens. It fits.
So for a shop sum like this, the cost of one, times how many, gives the total. You can do the next one yourself!
We have Dev, who is 32, and Tara, who is 20. We are asked about the difference in their ages, but 8 years ago.

board.text: Dev is 32, Tara is 20. Difference 8 years ago = ?

beats.say: Difference means the gap between the two ages: how much older one of them is than the other.
Think about this before any sum. 8 years ago, was the gap between them bigger, smaller, or the same as today?

ask.ifNot: Both of them were 8 years younger then. They step back together, so the gap between them does not move.

beats.say: Here is a fact worth keeping: the gap between two ages never changes. Every year, both people get exactly one year older.

spec.note: The extra piece is the gap between them

beats.say: So we only need the gap today. Dev's bar is Tara's bar plus an extra piece. 32 minus 20 is 12.
Don't just take my word for it. Go back 8 years: Dev was 32 minus 8, that is 24. Tara was 20 minus 8, that is 12.
And 24 minus 12 is 12. The very same gap!
So 8 years ago, the difference in their ages was 12 years.
So whenever a question asks for the difference in two ages, in any year at all, subtract the ages you know. The gap never changes.
The ages of Meera and Aditya are in the ratio 3 is to 4. Aditya is 28 years old, and we want Meera's age.
Look at the order carefully. Meera is named first, so Meera goes with the 3. Aditya is second, and goes with the 4.
As bars: Meera's age is 3 equal parts, and Aditya's is 4 parts of the same size. We know Aditya's whole bar is 28 years.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: So how do we find what one part is worth?

ask.ifNot: The 28 years belong to Aditya alone, and Aditya's bar has 4 parts. So we divide 28 by 4.

beats.say: 28 divided by 4 is 7, so each part is 7 years. Notice we did not add 3 and 4 this time, because 28 is not the total of both ages.

spec.note: Each piece is 7 years

beats.say: Meera has 3 of these parts. 3 times 7 is 21.
So Meera is 21 years old.
Check. Take 21 is to 28, and divide both by 7. We get 3 is to 4, the ratio in the question.
So when you are told one person's share, divide it by that person's parts to find one part. Then multiply for the other person.
Priya is 23 years old and Nikhil is 16. We want the sum of their ages after 8 years.

board.text: Priya is 23, Nikhil is 16. Sum after 8 years = ?

beats.say: Read the last part again: after 8 years. So we don't add the ages they have today. We add the ages they will have then.
Here is a bar for each of them. In 8 years, each bar grows by a piece of 8.

spec.note: Both bars grow by the same piece

beats.say: Who gets older in those 8 years?

ask.ifNot: Time passes for everybody. Priya gets 8 years older, and so does Nikhil.

beats.say: Priya will be 23 plus 8, which is 31. Nikhil will be 16 plus 8, which is 24.
Now add the two new ages. 31 plus 24 is 55.
So after 8 years, their ages add up to 55.
Here is a quick check. Today they add up to 39. Two people each gain 8 years, so the sum gains 16. And 39 plus 16 is 55.
The slip to avoid is adding the 8 only once. Two people means the years are added two times.
Two people here: Kavya, who is 9, and Siddharth, who is 24. The question asks what their ages will add up to after 4 years.

board.text: Kavya is 9, Siddharth is 24. Sum after 4 years = ?

beats.say: Read the last part again: after 4 years. So we don't add the ages they have today. We add the ages they will have then.
Here is a bar for each of them. In 4 years, each bar grows by a piece of 4.

spec.note: Both bars grow by the same piece

beats.say: Who gets older in those 4 years?

ask.ifNot: Time passes for everybody. Kavya gets 4 years older, and so does Siddharth.

beats.say: Kavya will be 9 plus 4, which is 13. Siddharth will be 24 plus 4, which is 28.
Now add the two new ages. 13 plus 28 is 41.
So after 4 years, their ages add up to 41.
Here is a quick check. Today they add up to 33. Two people each gain 4 years, so the sum gains 8. And 33 plus 8 is 41.
So remember: when years pass, they pass for everyone. Add the 4 years once for each person.

board.text: Vivek is 39, Tara is 19. Difference 3 years ago = ?

Don't just take my word for it. Go back 3 years: Vivek was 39 minus 3, that is 36. Tara was 19 minus 3, that is 16.
And 36 minus 16 is 20. The very same gap!

Here is a quick check. Today they add up to 43. Two people each gain 4 years, so the sum gains 8. And 43 plus 8 is 51.

Here is a shop sum with two parts. 7 rulers at 9 rupees each, and Riya pays with 83 rupees. How much change?

board.text: 7 rulers at Rs.9 each. Pays Rs.83.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 83 rupees pays for the rulers, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the rulers
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 7 rulers, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 7 rulers at 9 rupees each: that is 7 times 9. 7 times 9 is 63.
Careful: 63 is only the cost, not the answer. Riya paid 83. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 63 away from 83.

beats.say: From 83, take off the 63. That leaves 20.

A profit means it is sold for more than it cost, so the bottom bar is longer. That extra bit on the end is the profit.
The profit is 40 per cent. But 40 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 75 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the classic trap. Profit per cent is always worked out on the cost price, never on the selling price. And per cent means out of every 100.
Start with the friendly one, 10 per cent. 10 per cent is one tenth, so we divide by 10. 75 divided by 10 is 7.5.
Now, 40 per cent is just 10 per cent, 4 times over. 4 times 7.5 makes 30. That is the profit.
So the profit is 30 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 75 plus 30 is 105. So the selling price is 105 rupees.
Does that make sense? A profit should lift the selling price above the cost price, and 105 is 30 more than 75. It fits.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. Now you try one!

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 42 rupees equally among 6 sharpeners. Sharing equally is dividing.

beats.say: Think of the 6 times table. 6 times what makes 42? 6 times 7 is 42.
So one sharpener costs 7 rupees.
Check by building it back up. 6 sharpeners at 7 rupees each: 6 times 7 is 42. It fits.
So when you know the cost of many and want the cost of one, divide the total by how many. You can do the next one yourself!
Here is a shop sum with two parts. 3 pencils at 7 rupees each, and Ananya pays with 36 rupees. How much change?

board.text: 3 pencils at Rs.7 each. Pays Rs.36.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 36 rupees pays for the pencils, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the pencils
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 3 pencils, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 3 pencils at 7 rupees each: that is 3 times 7. 3 times 7 is 21.
Careful: 21 is only the cost, not the answer. Ananya paid 36. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 21 away from 36.

beats.say: From 36, take off the 21. That leaves 15.
So Ananya gets 15 rupees back.
A quick check. Cost plus change should give back the money paid: 21 plus 15 is 36. It works.
So a change sum takes two moves. First find the total cost. Then take it away from the money paid. Your turn next!
The pen set costs Siddharth 250 rupees: that is the cost price. Then it is sold at a profit of 50 per cent. What is the selling price?
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 250 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
A profit means it is sold for more than it cost, so the bottom bar is longer. That extra bit on the end is the profit.
The profit is 50 per cent. But 50 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 250 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
50 per cent is 50 out of every 100, and that is exactly one half. Half of 250 is 125. That is the profit.
So the profit is 125 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 250 plus 125 is 375. So the selling price is 375 rupees.
Does that make sense? A profit should lift the selling price above the cost price, and 375 is 125 more than 250. It fits.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. Now you try one!
Tara pays 800 rupees for a laptop. That is the cost price. It is sold at a loss of 25 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Let us draw it as two bars. On top, the cost price: 800 rupees. Underneath, the selling price, which we have to find.
A loss means it is sold for less than it cost, so the bottom bar is shorter. That missing bit is the loss.
The loss is 25 per cent. But 25 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 800 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the classic trap. Loss per cent is always worked out on the cost price, never on the selling price. And per cent means out of every 100.
4 lots of 25 make 100, so 25 per cent is one quarter. A quarter is half of a half. First, half of 800 is 400.
And half of 400 is 200. So 25 per cent of 800 is 200 rupees. That is the loss.
So the loss is 200 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 800 take away 200 is 600. So the selling price is 600 rupees.
Quick check. With a loss, the selling price must be smaller than the cost price. 600 is 200 below 800. Good.
So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. You can do the next one yourself!
15 stickers cost 150 rupees altogether. We want the cost of just one sticker.
Picture the 150 rupees as one long bar, cut into 15 equal pieces, one piece for each sticker. Every sticker costs the same.
So which sum finds the cost of one sticker?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 150 rupees equally among 15 stickers. Sharing equally is dividing.

beats.say: 150 is exactly 15 tens. So 150 divided by 15 is 10.
There it is: each sticker costs 10 rupees.
Check by building it back up. 15 stickers at 10 rupees each: 15 times 10 is 150. It fits.
So when you know the cost of many and want the cost of one, divide the total by how many. Now you try one!
3 bags of lentils, each one 3 kilograms 750 grams. Our job is to find what they weigh altogether, in grams.

board.text: 3 bags of lentils, each 3 kg 750 g

spec.note: Each bag weighs 3 kg 750 g

beats.say: One bag is written in two units at once, kilograms and grams, and those do not mix. We want grams, so let's turn the kilograms into grams. How many grams are in 1 kilogram?

ask.ifNot: Kilo means a thousand. So 1 kilogram is 1000 grams.

beats.say: Grams are tiny next to kilograms, so the number has to grow: we multiply by 1000. 3 kilograms is 3 times 1000, which is 3000 grams.
Do not lose the 750 grams that came with it. 3000 plus 750 is 3750 grams, so now one bag is written in a single unit.

spec.note: Each bag weighs 3 kg 750 g

beats.say: Every bag weighs 3750 grams, and there are 3 of them. What shall we work out?

ask.ifNot: There are 3 bags, and each one is the full 3750 grams. So we need 3 lots of 3750: a multiplication.

beats.say: Let's multiply in two easy pieces. 3 times 3000 is 9000, and 3 times 750 is 2250.
Add the two pieces: 9000 plus 2250 is 11250. So the 3 bags together weigh 11250 grams.
Quick sense check. The kilograms on their own came to 9000 grams. Our 11250 is a bit bigger, thanks to the extra 750 grams in every bag. Leaving those out is the classic slip.
So the plan for mixed units: first write one bag in a single unit, here grams. Then multiply by the number of bags.
A drum holds 20 litres of water, and each glass takes 300 millilitres. How many glasses can we fill?
Before any sums, check the units. Litres for the drum, millilitres for the glass. They do not mix, so one of them has to change. Which one?

ask.ifNot: We can only compare amounts that are in the same unit. Changing the litres into millilitres keeps every number whole, so that is the friendly choice.

beats.say: Each litre is 1000 millilitres. Smaller unit, so more of them: we multiply by 1000. 20 times 1000 gives 20000 millilitres in the drum.
Now both are in millilitres, so we want to know how many lots of 300 fit into 20000. Take two zeros off each to make it friendlier: how many lots of 3 fit into 200?
3 does not go into 200 exactly. 3 times 66 is 198, and that is as close as we can get without going over.
So 66 glasses use 19800 millilitres. Take that from 20000, and 200 millilitres are left over.
Here is the bit to think about. There are 200 millilitres left in the drum. Can we count one more glass?

ask.ifNot: A glass only counts when it is full, and a full one needs 300 millilitres. We have just 200 left, so that last bit stays in the drum.

beats.say: The leftover 200 millilitres is not enough for another glass. So 66 glasses can be filled.
Let's be sure. Glass number 67 would bring the total to 20100 millilitres, and that is more than the 20000 the drum holds. So 66 is right.
So the plan: same units first, then divide. And when something is left over, ask what the leftover means before you round.
Here is a rectangle, 17 centimetres long and 6 centimetres wide. We want its area.
Area is the space inside the shape: how many little squares would cover it. Which rule gives us that?

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides takes you along the edges, and that is the perimeter, the walk around. For the space inside we count rows of squares: length times width.

beats.say: Picture little squares, 1 centimetre each way. Every row holds 17 of them, and there are 6 rows. 6 rows of 17 is 17 times 6.
Split 17 into 10 and 7. 10 times 6 is 60, and 7 times 6 is 42. Together that makes 102.
That gives an area of 102 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area counts squares that cover the shape.
Check by undoing it. 102 shared into 6 rows gives 17 in each row, and that is our length. It fits.
Remember: area means the space inside, so multiply length by width. Adding the sides is for the walk around the edge.
40 millimetres. Same length, new unit: we want it in centimetres.
Start with the fact that links the two units. 1 centimetre is 10 millimetres. You can see it on your ruler: 10 tiny gaps inside every centimetre.
A centimetre is bigger than a millimetre. So will the number of centimetres be bigger or smaller than 40?

ask.ifNot: It takes 10 millimetres to make just 1 centimetre. A bigger unit means fewer of them, so the number goes down: we divide.

beats.say: Every 10 millimetres make 1 centimetre, so we count how many lots of 10 are in 40. 40 divided by 10 is 4.
So 40 millimetres is the same length as 4 centimetres.
Check by going back the other way. 4 centimetres, times 10, is 40 millimetres. Just what we started with.
Remember the idea, not just the rule. Bigger units mean fewer of them, so going up to a bigger unit we divide.
Aditya has 2 bags of lentils, and each bag weighs 2 kilograms 500 grams. We want the weight of all the bags together, in grams.

board.text: 2 bags of lentils, each 2 kg 500 g

spec.note: Each bag weighs 2 kg 500 g

beats.say: One bag is written in two units at once, kilograms and grams, and those do not mix. We want grams, so let's turn the kilograms into grams. How many grams are in 1 kilogram?

ask.ifNot: Kilo means a thousand. So 1 kilogram is 1000 grams.

beats.say: 1 kilogram is 1000 grams. A gram is much smaller than a kilogram, so we need many more of them: that is why we multiply. 2 times 1000 is 2000 grams.
Now put back the 500 grams that were already there. 2000 plus 500 makes 2500 grams. That is one bag, all in grams.

spec.note: Each bag weighs 2 kg 500 g

beats.say: Every bag weighs 2500 grams, and there are 2 of them. What shall we work out?

ask.ifNot: There are 2 bags, and each one is the full 2500 grams. So we need 2 lots of 2500: a multiplication.

beats.say: Doubling is easiest in two pieces. Double 2000 is 4000, and double 500 is 1000.
Add the two pieces: 4000 plus 1000 is 5000. So the 2 bags together weigh 5000 grams.
Quick sense check. The kilograms on their own came to 4000 grams. Our 5000 is a bit bigger, thanks to the extra 500 grams in every bag. Leaving those out is the classic slip.
So the plan for mixed units: first write one bag in a single unit, here grams. Then multiply by the number of bags.
We have a bucket with 15 litres of water in it, and glasses that hold 200 millilitres each. Let's find how many glasses it fills.
Before any sums, check the units. Litres for the bucket, millilitres for the glass. They do not mix, so one of them has to change. Which one?

ask.ifNot: We can only compare amounts that are in the same unit. Changing the litres into millilitres keeps every number whole, so that is the friendly choice.

beats.say: Each litre is 1000 millilitres. Smaller unit, so more of them: we multiply by 1000. 15 times 1000 gives 15000 millilitres in the bucket.
Now both amounts are in millilitres. How do we find how many 200 millilitre glasses fit into 15000 millilitres?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing the water out into equal glasses. Finding how many equal groups fit is a division.

beats.say: Dividing by 200 is easy with one friendly fact: 5 glasses of 200 millilitres make exactly 1000. So every litre fills 5 glasses.
There are 15 litres, with 5 glasses from each one. 15 times 5 is 75. So 75 glasses can be filled.
Check by pouring it back. 75 glasses of 200 millilitres is 75 times 200, which is 15000 millilitres. That is the whole bucket, with nothing left over.
Remember the order. Same units first, here millilitres. Then divide the big amount by the size of one glass.
Here is a square, and each side is 18 centimetres. We want its area.
Area is the space inside the shape: how many little squares would cover it. Which rule gives us that for a square?

ask.ifNot: 4 times the side is the walk around the edge, and that is the perimeter. For the space inside we count rows of little squares: side times side.

beats.say: In a square every side is the same. So each row holds 18 little squares, and there are 18 rows as well. That is 18 times 18.
Split 18 into 10 and 8. 18 times 10 is 180, and 18 times 8 is 144. Together that makes 324.
So the area is 324 square centimetres. Careful: 18 times 18 means 18 rows of 18. It is not the same as doubling 18.
Check by undoing it. 324 shared into 18 rows gives 18 in each row. That is our side again.
Remember: area of a square is side times side. Rows of little squares, all the same length.
7000 metres. Same length, new unit: we want it in kilometres.
Start with the fact that links the two units. 1 kilometre is 1000 metres. The clue is in the name: kilo means a thousand.
A kilometre is bigger than a metre. So will the number of kilometres be bigger or smaller than 7000?

ask.ifNot: It takes 1000 metres to make just 1 kilometre. A bigger unit means fewer of them, so the number goes down: we divide.

beats.say: Every 1000 metres make 1 kilometre, so we count how many lots of 1000 are in 7000. 7000 divided by 1000 is 7.
So 7000 metres is the same length as 7 kilometres.
Check by going back the other way. 7 kilometres, times 1000, is 7000 metres. Just what we started with.
So, small unit to a bigger unit: divide by how many small ones make one big one. Bigger unit, smaller number.

So Vivek gets 20 rupees back.
Check it the shopkeeper's way. The cost, 72, plus the change, 20, should make the 92 that was paid. It does.
Two moves, every time: work out the total cost, then subtract it from what was paid. You can do the next one yourself!

20 pens cost 60 rupees altogether. We want the cost of just one pen.
Think of the 60 rupees as a bar shared into 20 equal pieces. Each piece is the price of one pen.
So which sum finds the cost of one pen?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 60 rupees equally among 20 pens. Sharing equally is dividing.

beats.say: Dividing by 20 is easier in two steps: divide by 10, then by 2. First, 60 divided by 10 is 6.
Then 6 divided by 2 is 3. So 60 divided by 20 is 3.
So one pen costs 3 rupees.
Check by building it back up. 20 pens at 3 rupees each: 20 times 3 is 60. It fits.

9 pens, and every one costs 7 rupees. How much does Arjun pay altogether?
Let us lay it out like a shop bill. One pen costs 7 rupees, and there are 9 of them.
So which sum gives the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 9 pens costs 7 rupees. That is 7 rupees, 9 times over, so we multiply.

beats.say: Same price, 9 times, so it is a times sum. 9 times 7 is 63.
So Arjun pays 63 rupees altogether.
Let us check by sharing it back out. 63 rupees, in lots of 7 rupees, gives 9 pens. It fits.

Siddharth has 5 bags of rice, and each bag weighs 2 kilograms 750 grams. We want the weight of all the bags together, in grams.

board.text: 5 bags of rice, each 2 kg 750 g

spec.note: Each bag weighs 2 kg 750 g

We have a drum with 12 litres of water in it, and glasses that hold 200 millilitres each. Let's find how many glasses it fills.

ask.ifNot: We can only compare amounts that are in the same unit. Changing the litres into millilitres keeps every number whole, so that is the friendly choice.

beats.say: 1 litre is 1000 millilitres. A millilitre is much smaller, so we need many more of them, and that means multiply. 12 times 1000 is 12000 millilitres.
Now both amounts are in millilitres. How do we find how many 200 millilitre glasses fit into 12000 millilitres?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing the water out into equal glasses. Finding how many equal groups fit is a division.

beats.say: Here is a friendly fact to help. 200 times 5 is exactly 1000, so each litre of water fills 5 glasses.
There are 12 litres, with 5 glasses from each one. 12 times 5 is 60. So 60 glasses can be filled.
Check by pouring it back. 60 glasses of 200 millilitres is 60 times 200, which is 12000 millilitres. That is the whole drum, with nothing left over.
Remember the order. Same units first, here millilitres. Then divide the big amount by the size of one glass.

Remember the idea, not just the rule. Bigger units mean fewer of them, so going up to a bigger unit we divide.
