ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 27 away from 37.

beats.say: Count up from 27 to 37. That is 10 more.
So Neha gets 10 rupees back.
Check it the shopkeeper's way. The cost, 27, plus the change, 10, should make the 37 that was paid. It does.
So a change sum takes two moves. First find the total cost. Then take it away from the money paid. Now you try one!
Nikhil pays 80 rupees for a bag. That is the cost price. It is sold at a profit of 20 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Picture two bars, one under the other. The cost price, 80 rupees, is on top. The selling price is below, with a question mark for now.
With a profit, the selling price is bigger than the cost price. So the bottom bar sticks out, and the bit that sticks out is the profit.
The profit is 20 per cent. But 20 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 80 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
Start with the friendly one, 10 per cent. 10 per cent is one tenth, so we divide by 10. 80 divided by 10 is 8.
20 per cent is 2 lots of 10 per cent. 2 times 8 is 16. That is the profit.
So the profit is 16 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 80 plus 16 is 96. So the selling price is 96 rupees.
Quick check. With a profit, the selling price must be bigger than the cost price. 96 is 16 above 80. Good.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. Your turn next!
Riya pays 600 rupees for a tablet. That is the cost price. It is sold at a loss of 20 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Picture two bars, one under the other. The cost price, 600 rupees, is on top. The selling price is below, with a question mark for now.
With a loss, the selling price is smaller than the cost price. So the bottom bar stops short, and the gap is the loss.
The loss is 20 per cent. But 20 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 600 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Loss per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
Start with the friendly one, 10 per cent. 10 per cent is one tenth, so we divide by 10. 600 divided by 10 is 60.
Now, 20 per cent is just 10 per cent, 2 times over. 2 times 60 makes 120. That is the loss.
So the loss is 120 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 600 take away 120 is 480. So the selling price is 480 rupees.
Does that make sense? A loss should drop the selling price below the cost price, and 480 is 120 less than 600. It fits.
So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. Your turn next!
Here we know the price of the whole lot: 15 notebooks for 135 rupees. Our job is to find the price of one notebook.
Think of the 135 rupees as a bar shared into 15 equal pieces. Each piece is the price of one notebook.
So which sum finds the cost of one notebook?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 135 rupees equally among 15 notebooks. Sharing equally is dividing.

beats.say: Try 10 lots first. 15 times 10 is 150. That is a little too much.
Take one lot of 15 off: 150 minus 15 is 135. So it is 9 lots, one fewer than 10.
So one notebook costs 9 rupees.
Check by building it back up. 15 notebooks at 9 rupees each: 15 times 9 is 135. It fits.
Cost of many, and you want the cost of one? Divide the total cost by the number of things. Your turn next!
2 bags of lentils, each one 3 kilograms 750 grams. Our job is to find what they weigh altogether, in grams.

board.text: 2 bags of lentils, each 3 kg 750 g

spec.note: Each bag weighs 3 kg 750 g

beats.say: Look at how one bag is written: kilograms and grams mixed together. The answer must be in grams, so we change the kilograms. How many grams make 1 kilogram?

ask.ifNot: Kilo means a thousand. So 1 kilogram is 1000 grams.

beats.say: Grams are tiny next to kilograms, so the number has to grow: we multiply by 1000. 3 kilograms is 3 times 1000, which is 3000 grams.
Do not lose the 750 grams that came with it. 3000 plus 750 is 3750 grams, so now one bag is written in a single unit.

spec.note: Each bag weighs 3 kg 750 g

beats.say: Every bag weighs 3750 grams, and there are 2 of them. What shall we work out?

ask.ifNot: There are 2 bags, and each one is the full 3750 grams. So we need 2 lots of 3750: a multiplication.

beats.say: Doubling is easiest in two pieces. Double 3000 is 6000, and double 750 is 1500.
Add the two pieces: 6000 plus 1500 is 7500. So the 2 bags together weigh 7500 grams.
Does that make sense? The kilograms alone gave 6000 grams, and our answer is a little more, because every bag has 750 extra grams. Forgetting those extra grams is the slip to watch for.
Remember the order: get everything into one unit first, then do the multiplying. Units first, sums second.
A tank holds 8 litres of water, and each glass takes 300 millilitres. How many glasses can we fill?
Look at the units first. The tank is in litres, the glass is in millilitres, and those two do not mix. Which shall we change?

ask.ifNot: We can only compare amounts that are in the same unit. Changing the litres into millilitres keeps every number whole, so that is the friendly choice.

beats.say: 1 litre is 1000 millilitres. A millilitre is much smaller, so we need many more of them, and that means multiply. 8 times 1000 is 8000 millilitres.
Now both are in millilitres, so we want to know how many lots of 300 fit into 8000. Take two zeros off each to make it friendlier: how many lots of 3 fit into 80?
3 does not go into 80 exactly. 3 times 26 is 78, and that is as close as we can get without going over.
So 26 glasses use 7800 millilitres. Take that from 8000, and 200 millilitres are left over.
Here is the bit to think about. There are 200 millilitres left in the tank. Can we count one more glass?

ask.ifNot: A glass only counts when it is full, and a full one needs 300 millilitres. We have just 200 left, so that last bit stays in the tank.

beats.say: The leftover 200 millilitres is not enough for another glass. So 26 glasses can be filled.
Let's be sure. Glass number 27 would bring the total to 8100 millilitres, and that is more than the 8000 the tank holds. So 26 is right.
Remember: get both amounts into millilitres, see how many glasses fit, and never round up a glass that is not full.
Our shape is a square with sides of 8 centimetres. The question asks for its area.
Area is the space inside the shape: how many little squares would cover it. Which rule gives us that for a square?

ask.ifNot: 4 times the side is the walk around the edge, and that is the perimeter. For the space inside we count rows of little squares: side times side.

beats.say: In a square every side is the same. So each row holds 8 little squares, and there are 8 rows as well. That is 8 times 8.
8 times 8 is 64. That is a tables fact worth knowing by heart.
So the area is 64 square centimetres. Careful: 8 times 8 means 8 rows of 8. It is not the same as doubling 8.
Check by undoing it. 64 shared into 8 rows gives 8 in each row. That is our side again.
So for the area of a square, multiply the side by itself. 4 times the side is a different question, the perimeter.
We have 90 millimetres, and we want to say the same length in centimetres.
Start with the fact that links the two units. 1 centimetre is 10 millimetres. You can see it on your ruler: 10 tiny gaps inside every centimetre.
A centimetre is bigger than a millimetre. So will the number of centimetres be bigger or smaller than 90?

ask.ifNot: It takes 10 millimetres to make just 1 centimetre. A bigger unit means fewer of them, so the number goes down: we divide.

beats.say: We are bundling the millimetres into groups of 10, one group for each centimetre. 90 divided by 10 is 9.
So 90 millimetres is the same length as 9 centimetres.
Check by going back the other way. 9 centimetres, times 10, is 90 millimetres. Just what we started with.
Remember the idea, not just the rule. Bigger units mean fewer of them, so going up to a bigger unit we divide.
Dev buys 8 sharpeners at 10 rupees each, and hands over 105 rupees. We want the change that comes back.

board.text: 8 sharpeners at Rs.10 each. Pays Rs.105.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 105 rupees pays for the sharpeners, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the sharpeners
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 8 sharpeners, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 8 sharpeners at 10 rupees each: that is 8 times 10. 8 times 10 is 80.
Careful: 80 is only the cost, not the answer. Dev paid 105. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 80 away from 105.

beats.say: From 105, take off the 80. That leaves 25.
So Dev gets 25 rupees back.
Check it the shopkeeper's way. The cost, 80, plus the change, 25, should make the 105 that was paid. It does.
Two moves, every time: work out the total cost, then subtract it from what was paid. Now you try one!
Kavya pays 40 rupees for a book. That is the cost price. It is sold at a profit of 50 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 40 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
A profit means it is sold for more than it cost, so the bottom bar is longer. That extra bit on the end is the profit.
The profit is 50 per cent. But 50 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 40 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
50 per cent is 50 out of every 100, and that is exactly one half. Half of 40 is 20. That is the profit.
So the profit is 20 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 40 plus 20 is 60. So the selling price is 60 rupees.
Does that make sense? A profit should lift the selling price above the cost price, and 60 is 20 more than 40. It fits.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. Your turn next!
Sahil pays 200 rupees for a phone. That is the cost price. It is sold at a loss of 20 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 200 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
A loss means it is sold for less than it cost, so the bottom bar is shorter. That missing bit is the loss.
The loss is 20 per cent. But 20 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 200 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Loss per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
10 per cent is the easy one: it is one tenth. 200 divided by 10 is 20.
Now, 20 per cent is just 10 per cent, 2 times over. 2 times 20 makes 40. That is the loss.
So the loss is 40 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 200 take away 40 is 160. So the selling price is 160 rupees.
Does that make sense? A loss should drop the selling price below the cost price, and 160 is 40 less than 200. It fits.
So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. Your turn next!
Here we know the price of the whole lot: 6 pencils for 48 rupees. Our job is to find the price of one pencil.
Think of the 48 rupees as a bar shared into 6 equal pieces. Each piece is the price of one pencil.
So which sum finds the cost of one pencil?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 48 rupees equally among 6 pencils. Sharing equally is dividing.

beats.say: Think of the 6 times table. 6 times what makes 48? 6 times 8 is 48.
So one pencil costs 8 rupees.
Check by building it back up. 6 pencils at 8 rupees each: 6 times 8 is 48. It fits.
So when you know the cost of many and want the cost of one, divide the total by how many. Your turn next!
3 x, plus 8, plus 3 x, minus 2. That is quite a mouthful. Let's tidy it up, so it says the same thing in fewer pieces.
Think of x as a box with a secret number of sweets inside. 3 x is 3 boxes, and 3 x is 3 more boxes. The plain numbers are loose sweets. What can we count together?

choices: a box and some loose sweets
ask.ifNot: Boxes go with boxes, and loose sweets go with loose sweets. We cannot add a box to a loose sweet, because we do not know how many are inside the box.

beats.say: First the x family. 3 lots of x and 3 more lots of x make 6 lots of x.
Now the plain numbers. Careful: the sign in front of a number belongs to that number. So this is 8 minus 2, which is 6.
So we have 6 x and 6. Here is where people slip. Can we squash those two into one term?

choices: No, they are not like terms
ask.ifNot: 6 x means 6 lots of a hidden number. 6 is a plain number. They are different families, so they stay side by side.

beats.say: So the short form is 6 x plus 6. Same value, far fewer pieces.
Let's test it with a number. Say x is 1. The long one is 3 plus 8 plus 3 minus 2, which is 12. The short one is 6 plus 6, also 12. They match.
The plan every time: x terms with x terms, numbers with numbers, and each sign stays with its own term.
Two letters this time. x is 3 and y is 6. Our job is to find the value of 5 x plus 1 y.
First, what does 5 x turn into when x is 3?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 5 x means 5 times x, and here that is 5 times 3.

beats.say: So we swap each letter for its number. 5 x becomes 5 times 3, and 1 y becomes 1 times 6.
Now we have two multiplications and one addition. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying comes before adding. So we work out each times first, and only then add the two answers.

beats.say: 5 times 3 is 15. And 1 y is just one single y, so that is 6.
Now add them. 15 plus 6 is 21. So 5 x plus 1 y is worth 21.
So for any question like this: swap each letter for its number, do the times first, then add. And 5 x is 5 times x, never the two digits side by side.
A number game! Our number is 20. We multiply it by 5, and then we add 11. Let's take it one step at a time.
Which step comes first?

ask.ifNot: Read the recipe again: multiply it by 5 comes before add 11. So first we work out 20 times 5.

beats.say: 20 times 5 is 100.
Next the recipe says add 11. What do we add it to?

ask.ifNot: We add it to the number we are holding now, not the one we started with. Right now we are holding 100.

beats.say: 100 plus 11 is 111. That is what we get.
Here is the clever bit. If we call the starting number n, the whole recipe is 5 n plus 11. That is all algebra is: a recipe, with a letter standing for the number.
Put 20 in for n. 5 times 20, plus 11, is 111. The same answer. Just never add the 5 and the 11 first, because that changes the recipe.
So: follow the steps in the order they are given, one at a time, and always carry on from the number you have reached.
We know that x is 6. We want the value of 4 x, plus 11, minus 5.
First, what does 4 x turn into when x is 6?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 4 x means 4 times x, and here that is 4 times 6.

beats.say: So we rub out the x and write 6 in its place, with a times sign. 4 times 6, plus 11, minus 5.
Three jobs here: a times, a plus and a minus. Which one goes first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying always goes before adding and taking away. So 4 times 6 comes first.

beats.say: 4 times 6 is 24. So now we have 24, plus 11, minus 5.
Now we go left to right. 24 plus 11 is 35. Then 35 minus 5 is 30.
So when x is 6, the whole thing is worth 30. The plan: swap the letter for its number, multiply first, then work left to right.
Find the square root of 484. First, let's be sure what that is asking.
What is a square root question really asking?

ask.ifNot: A square root is not a half. It asks: which number, multiplied by itself, makes 484?

beats.say: Yes. The same number goes in both boxes: something times itself makes 484. Think of 484 tiles laid out as a perfect square. How long is one side?
484 is too big for our tables, so we trap it between two squares we know. 20 times 20 is 400. 30 times 30 is 900.
484 sits between 400 and 900. So where is our number?

ask.ifNot: Look at the two lines. 484 is more than 400 and less than 900. So its root is more than 20 and less than 30.

beats.say: Now the clever clue: the last digit. 484 ends in 4. 2 times 2 is 4, and 8 times 8 is 64: both end in 4.
So our number ends in 2 or 8: it is 22 or 28. Now, 484 is closer to 400 than to 900. Which one shall we try?

ask.ifNot: 400 is the square of 20, and 484 is close to it. So we want the one nearer to 20, and that is 22.

beats.say: Let's test 22. Break the second 22 into 20 and 2. 22 times 20 is 440, and 22 times 2 is 44.
440 plus 44 is 484. That is our number exactly!
So the square root of 484 is 22.
That is the plan every time: squeeze it between two tens, read the last digit, and test your best guess by multiplying.
Which of these is a perfect square: 144, 150, 147 or 145? Let's remember what a perfect square is first.
A perfect square is a number of tiles that makes a full square, with nothing left over. Like 9 tiles, in 3 rows of 3.
Let's walk up the squares until we reach our numbers. 11 times 11 is 121: too small.
The next square is 12 times 12. What does that make?

ask.ifNot: 12 times 12 is 12 lots of 12. From the 12 times table, that is 144.

beats.say: 12 times 12 is 144, and there it is in our list! 144 tiles make a square with 12 on each side.
What about the others? The very next square is 13 times 13, which is 169. So 150, 147 and 145 are stuck in the gap between two squares.
So the perfect square is 144.
To test for a perfect square, walk up the squares and see whether you land exactly on the number.
Let's read it together. The square root of x, plus 12, equals 18. Under that root sign sits x, and we want it.
The root of x is not alone on the left. Something is sitting next to it. What should we move out of the way first?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side again. The root of x has a plus 12 hanging on to it. That goes first, and the root sign waits until the end.

beats.say: Plus 12 is undone by minus 12. Whatever we do on the left, we do on the right as well.
On the left, only the root of x is left. On the right, 18 minus 12 is 6.
Don't put your pencil down yet. 6 is only the root of x. Which sum takes us from the root back to x?

ask.ifNot: A square root is the number that multiplies by itself to make x. So we go back the other way: x is 6 times 6, not 6 times 2.

beats.say: Picture a square of tiles, 6 rows with 6 tiles in each row. The side of the square is the root. All the tiles together are x.
6 times 6 is 36. So x is 36. There is our hidden number!
Let's check it. The square root of 36 is 6, and 6 plus 12 is 18. It fits perfectly.
So the plan for a puzzle like this: first get the root on its own, then square it to find x.
We want the square of 9. It gets its name from a shape, so let's start with the shape.
Look at this square of tiles: 9 rows, with 9 tiles in each row. Count all the tiles, and you have the square of 9.
So which sum gives us the square of 9?

ask.ifNot: Look at the tiles. There are 9 rows, and each row has 9 tiles. That is 9 lots of 9, so 9 times 9.

beats.say: Careful with that little 2 up in the air. It never means times 2. It tells us to multiply the number by itself.
And what is 9 times 9? Use your tables.

ask.ifNot: Count up in lots of 9, 9 times over. You land on 81.

beats.say: 9 times 9 is 81. So the square of 9 is 81.
A quick check, going backwards: the square root of 81 is 9, because 9 times 9 is 81.
Remember: the square of a number is that number times itself, like the tiles in a square.
Find the square root of 196. First, let's be sure what that is asking.
What is a square root question really asking?

ask.ifNot: A square root is not a half. It asks: which number, multiplied by itself, makes 196?

beats.say: So we need one number for both boxes. Picture 196 tiles arranged in a perfect square: the square root is the length of its side.
196 is too big for our tables, so we trap it between two squares we know. 10 times 10 is 100. 20 times 20 is 400.
196 sits between 100 and 400. So where is our number?

ask.ifNot: Look at the two lines. 196 is more than 100 and less than 400. So its root is more than 10 and less than 20.

beats.say: Now the clever clue: the last digit. 196 ends in 6. 4 times 4 is 16, and 6 times 6 is 36: both end in 6.
So our number ends in 4 or 6: it is 14 or 16. Now, 196 is closer to 100 than to 400. Which one shall we try?

ask.ifNot: 100 is the square of 10, and 196 is close to it. So we want the one nearer to 10, and that is 14.

beats.say: Let's test 14. Break the second 14 into 10 and 4. 14 times 10 is 140, and 14 times 4 is 56.
140 plus 56 is 196. That is our number exactly!
So the square root of 196 is 14.
That is the plan every time: squeeze it between two tens, read the last digit, and test your best guess by multiplying.
Here is our puzzle. The square root of x, plus 15, equals 22. We are hunting for x, the number hiding under the root sign.
Think of the square root of x as one closed box. The box plus 15 makes 22. So what do we clear away first?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side again. The root of x has a plus 15 hanging on to it. That goes first, and the root sign waits until the end.

beats.say: To undo plus 15, we take away 15. And to keep the balance level, we take it from both sides.
Now the root of x stands alone. And 22 minus 15 gives us 7.
Now the trap. We have found the square root of x, and that is 7. We have not found x yet! What undoes a square root?

ask.ifNot: A square root is the number that multiplies by itself to make x. So we go back the other way: x is 7 times 7, not 7 times 2.

beats.say: Picture a square of tiles, 7 rows with 7 tiles in each row. The side of the square is the root. All the tiles together are x.
From our tables, 7 times 7 is 49. So x equals 49.
Let's check it. The square root of 49 is 7, and 7 plus 15 is 22. It fits perfectly.
Two moves, in order: undo the plus, then undo the root by squaring. Your turn next!
Find the square of 8. That little word, square, is a big clue. So let's draw one.
Here is a square made of tiles. It has 8 rows, and 8 tiles in every row. The square of 8 is the number of tiles in it.
Which sum counts all the tiles in that square?

ask.ifNot: Look at the tiles. There are 8 rows, and each row has 8 tiles. That is 8 lots of 8, so 8 times 8.

beats.say: Careful with that little 2 up in the air. It never means times 2. It tells us to multiply the number by itself.
And what is 8 times 8? Use your tables.

ask.ifNot: Count up in lots of 8, 8 times over. You land on 64.

beats.say: 8 times 8 is 64. So the square of 8 is 64.
A quick check, going backwards: the square root of 64 is 8, because 8 times 8 is 64.
So, to square a number, multiply it by itself. Never by 2!
We want the square root of 36. Before we hunt for it, what does a square root mean?
What is a square root question really asking?

ask.ifNot: A square root is not a half. It asks: which number, multiplied by itself, makes 36?

beats.say: So we need one number for both boxes. Picture 36 tiles arranged in a perfect square: the square root is the length of its side.
Let's test some numbers. 5 times 5 is 25. That is too small.
Too small, so we go one bigger. What is 6 times 6?

ask.ifNot: 6 times 6 means 6 lots of 6. Count up in lots of 6 and you land on 36.

beats.say: 6 times 6 is exactly 36. Look: 36 tiles make a square with 6 on each side.
So the square root of 36 is 6.
Remember: a square root is the side of the square. Find the number that, times itself, gives what you started with.
We want the square root of 900. Before we hunt for it, what does a square root mean?
Which of these is the square root asking for?

ask.ifNot: A square root is not a half. It asks: which number, multiplied by itself, makes 900?

beats.say: Yes. The same number goes in both boxes: something times itself makes 900. Think of 900 tiles laid out as a perfect square. How long is one side?
900 ends in two zeros. Cover them for a moment and we see 9. Which number, times itself, makes 9?

ask.ifNot: Try your tables: 3 times 3 is 9.

beats.say: 3 times 3 is 9. So 3 tens times 3 tens is 9 hundreds: 30 times 30 is 900.
So the square root of 900 is 30. There it is!
Picture it: 30 rows with 30 tiles in each row is 900 tiles. A perfect square.
So when a number ends in two zeros, find the root of the front part, then put one zero back.
Look at this one. The square root of x, plus 9, makes 20. Our job is to find x itself.
The root of x is not alone on the left. Something is sitting next to it. What should we move out of the way first?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side again. The root of x has a plus 9 hanging on to it. That goes first, and the root sign waits until the end.

beats.say: Plus 9 is undone by minus 9. Whatever we do on the left, we do on the right as well.
Now the root of x stands alone. And 20 minus 9 gives us 11.
Don't put your pencil down yet. 11 is only the root of x. Which sum takes us from the root back to x?

ask.ifNot: A square root is the number that multiplies by itself to make x. So we go back the other way: x is 11 times 11, not 11 times 2.

beats.say: Here is why. Build a square with 11 rows of 11 tiles. Its side is the square root, and the number of tiles in it is x.
11 times 11 is a big one, so we split it. 11 times 10 is 110, and 11 times 1 is 11.
110 plus 11 is 121. So x is 121. There is our hidden number!
Good mathematicians always check. Put 121 in place of x: its square root is 11, and 11 plus 9 is 20. It works.
Two moves, in order: undo the plus, then undo the root by squaring. Your turn next!
We want the square of 11. It gets its name from a shape, so let's start with the shape.
Here is a square made of tiles. It has 11 rows, and 11 tiles in every row. The square of 11 is the number of tiles in it.
Which sum counts all the tiles in that square?

ask.ifNot: Look at the tiles. There are 11 rows, and each row has 11 tiles. That is 11 lots of 11, so 11 times 11.

beats.say: Here is the trap to dodge. The little 2 does not mean times 2. It means the number is written twice and multiplied.
11 times 11 is not in our tables, so we break the second 11 into 10 and 1.
11 times 10 is 110. And 11 times 1 is 11. What do they make together?

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly. Add the ones first, then the tens, then the hundreds. 110 plus 11 comes to 121.

beats.say: 110 plus 11 is 121. So the square of 11 is 121.
And if we go backwards, the square root of 121 brings us home to 11. Square and square root undo each other.
So, to square a number, multiply it by itself. Never by 2!
We want the square root of 1156. Before we hunt for it, what does a square root mean?
Which of these is the square root asking for?

ask.ifNot: A square root is not a half. It asks: which number, multiplied by itself, makes 1156?

beats.say: Yes. The same number goes in both boxes: something times itself makes 1156. Think of 1156 tiles laid out as a perfect square. How long is one side?
1156 is too big for our tables, so we trap it between two squares we know. 30 times 30 is 900. 40 times 40 is 1600.
1156 sits between 900 and 1600. So where is our number?

ask.ifNot: Look at the two lines. 1156 is more than 900 and less than 1600. So its root is more than 30 and less than 40.

beats.say: Now the clever clue: the last digit. 1156 ends in 6. 4 times 4 is 16, and 6 times 6 is 36: both end in 6.
So our number ends in 4 or 6: it is 34 or 36. Now, 1156 is closer to 900 than to 1600. Which one shall we try?

Here is a long expression. 11 x, plus 3, plus 3 x, plus 5. Simplify means write it shorter, without changing what it is worth.

Two letters this time. x is 6 and y is 2. Our job is to find the value of 5 x plus 1 y.

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 5 x means 5 times x, and here that is 5 times 6.

ask.ifNot: Multiplying comes before adding. So we work out each times first, and only then add the two answers.

A number game! Our number is 7. We multiply it by 5, and then we add 14. Let's take it one step at a time.
Which step comes first?

ask.ifNot: Read the recipe again: multiply it by 5 comes before add 14. So first we work out 7 times 5.

Next the recipe says add 14. What do we add it to?

ask.ifNot: We add it to the number we are holding now, not the one we started with. Right now we are holding 35.

We know that x is 7. We want the value of 8 x, plus 8, minus 6.

What is a square root question really asking?

ask.ifNot: A square root is not a half. It asks: which number, multiplied by itself, makes 961?

961 sits between 900 and 1600. So where is our number?

ask.ifNot: Look at the two lines. 961 is more than 900 and less than 1600. So its root is more than 30 and less than 40.

ask.ifNot: 900 is the square of 30, and 961 is close to it. So we want the one nearer to 30, and that is 31.

Let's read it together. The square root of x, plus 4, equals 11. Under that root sign sits x, and we want it.

Find the square of 6. That little word, square, is a big clue. So let's draw one.

Now the trap. We have found the square root of x, and that is 14. We have not found x yet! What undoes a square root?

ask.ifNot: A square root is the number that multiplies by itself to make x. So we go back the other way: x is 14 times 14, not 14 times 2.

beats.say: Think of a big square of tiles, 14 along each side. The side is the root, and all the tiles together are x. So x is 14 times 14.
14 times 14 is a big one, so we split it. 14 times 10 is 140, and 14 times 4 is 56.
Add them up: 140 plus 56 makes 196. So x equals 196.
Let's check it. The square root of 196 is 14, and 14 plus 9 is 23. It fits perfectly.
Remember the two steps. Clear away what is added, then multiply the root by itself.
Here is our puzzle. The square root of x, plus 7, equals 16. We are hunting for x, the number hiding under the root sign.
The root of x is not alone on the left. Something is sitting next to it. What should we move out of the way first?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side again. The root of x has a plus 7 hanging on to it. That goes first, and the root sign waits until the end.

beats.say: To undo plus 7, we take away 7. And to keep the balance level, we take it from both sides.
Now the root of x stands alone. And 16 minus 7 gives us 9.
Now the trap. We have found the square root of x, and that is 9. We have not found x yet! What undoes a square root?

ask.ifNot: A square root is the number that multiplies by itself to make x. So we go back the other way: x is 9 times 9, not 9 times 2.

beats.say: Here is why. Build a square with 9 rows of 9 tiles. Its side is the square root, and the number of tiles in it is x.
9 times 9 is 81. So x is 81. There is our hidden number!
Good mathematicians always check. Put 81 in place of x: its square root is 9, and 9 plus 7 is 16. It works.
Two moves, in order: undo the plus, then undo the root by squaring. Your turn next!
Find the square root of 361. First, let's be sure what that is asking.
What is a square root question really asking?

ask.ifNot: A square root is not a half. It asks: which number, multiplied by itself, makes 361?

beats.say: So we need one number for both boxes. Picture 361 tiles arranged in a perfect square: the square root is the length of its side.
361 is too big for our tables, so we trap it between two squares we know. 10 times 10 is 100. 20 times 20 is 400.
361 sits between 100 and 400. So where is our number?

ask.ifNot: Look at the two lines. 361 is more than 100 and less than 400. So its root is more than 10 and less than 20.

beats.say: Now the clever clue: the last digit. 361 ends in 1. 1 times 1 is 1, and 9 times 9 is 81: both end in 1.
So our number ends in 1 or 9: it is 11 or 19. Now, 361 is closer to 400 than to 100. Which one shall we try?

ask.ifNot: 400 is the square of 20, and 361 is close to it. So we want the one nearer to 20, and that is 19.

beats.say: Let's test 19. Break the second 19 into 10 and 9. 19 times 10 is 190, and 19 times 9 is 171.
190 plus 171 is 361. That is our number exactly!
So the square root of 361 is 19.
So for a big square root: trap it between two tens, let the last digit pick the candidates, then multiply to make sure.
Here is our puzzle. The square root of x, plus 16, equals 30. We are hunting for x, the number hiding under the root sign.
The root of x is not alone on the left. Something is sitting next to it. What should we move out of the way first?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side again. The root of x has a plus 16 hanging on to it. That goes first, and the root sign waits until the end.

beats.say: So we subtract 16. Both sides, remember, or the balance tips.
On the left, only the root of x is left. On the right, 30 minus 16 is 14.
Don't put your pencil down yet. 14 is only the root of x. Which sum takes us from the root back to x?

ask.ifNot: A square root is the number that multiplies by itself to make x. So we go back the other way: x is 14 times 14, not 14 times 2.

beats.say: Think of a big square of tiles, 14 along each side. The side is the root, and all the tiles together are x. So x is 14 times 14.
14 times 14 is a big one, so we split it. 14 times 10 is 140, and 14 times 4 is 56.
140 plus 56 is 196. So x is 196. There is our hidden number!
Let's check it. The square root of 196 is 14, and 14 plus 16 is 30. It fits perfectly.
Two moves, in order: undo the plus, then undo the root by squaring. Your turn next!
Find the square of 25. That little word, square, is a big clue. So let's draw one.
A 25 by 25 square is too big for our board, so here is a baby one: 3 rows of 3 tiles. 3 times 3 is 9 tiles, so the square of 3 is 9.
Our square is the same idea, only bigger: 25 rows, with 25 tiles in each row. So which sum gives the square of 25?

ask.ifNot: Think of the square: 25 rows, and 25 tiles in every row. That is 25 lots of 25, so 25 times 25.

beats.say: Here is the trap to dodge. The little 2 does not mean times 2. It means the number is written twice and multiplied.
25 times 25 is not in our tables, so we break the second 25 into 20 and 5.
25 times 20 is 500. And 25 times 5 is 125. What do they make together?

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly. Add the ones first, then the tens, then the hundreds. 500 plus 125 comes to 625.

beats.say: 500 plus 125 is 625. So the square of 25 is 625.
And if we go backwards, the square root of 625 brings us home to 25. Square and square root undo each other.
Remember: the square of a number is that number times itself, like the tiles in a square.
Here is our puzzle. The square root of x, plus 20, equals 29. We are hunting for x, the number hiding under the root sign.
Think of the square root of x as one closed box. The box plus 20 makes 29. So what do we clear away first?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side again. The root of x has a plus 20 hanging on to it. That goes first, and the root sign waits until the end.

beats.say: So we subtract 20. Both sides, remember, or the balance tips.
Now the root of x stands alone. And 29 minus 20 gives us 9.
Careful, this is where many people stop! 9 is the square root of x, not x. So how do we get x from 9?

ask.ifNot: A square root is the number that multiplies by itself to make x. So we go back the other way: x is 9 times 9, not 9 times 2.

beats.say: Picture a square of tiles, 9 rows with 9 tiles in each row. The side of the square is the root. All the tiles together are x.
From our tables, 9 times 9 is 81. So x equals 81.
Let's check it. The square root of 81 is 9, and 9 plus 20 is 29. It fits perfectly.
Two moves, in order: undo the plus, then undo the root by squaring. Your turn next!
Let's read it together. The square root of x, plus 11, equals 23. Under that root sign sits x, and we want it.
Before we touch the root sign, we want the root of x standing by itself. What is in its way?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side again. The root of x has a plus 11 hanging on to it. That goes first, and the root sign waits until the end.

beats.say: To undo plus 11, we take away 11. And to keep the balance level, we take it from both sides.
Now the root of x stands alone. And 23 minus 11 gives us 12.
Now the trap. We have found the square root of x, and that is 12. We have not found x yet! What undoes a square root?

ask.ifNot: A square root is the number that multiplies by itself to make x. So we go back the other way: x is 12 times 12, not 12 times 2.

beats.say: Picture a square of tiles, 12 rows with 12 tiles in each row. The side of the square is the root. All the tiles together are x.
12 times 12 is a big one, so we split it. 12 times 10 is 120, and 12 times 2 is 24.
120 plus 24 is 144. So x is 144. There is our hidden number!
Good mathematicians always check. Put 144 in place of x: its square root is 12, and 12 plus 11 is 23. It works.
Two moves, in order: undo the plus, then undo the root by squaring. Your turn next!
Here is our puzzle. The square root of x, plus 9, equals 21. We are hunting for x, the number hiding under the root sign.
Think of the square root of x as one closed box. The box plus 9 makes 21. So what do we clear away first?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side again. The root of x has a plus 9 hanging on to it. That goes first, and the root sign waits until the end.

beats.say: To undo plus 9, we take away 9. And to keep the balance level, we take it from both sides.
Now the root of x stands alone. And 21 minus 9 gives us 12.
Don't put your pencil down yet. 12 is only the root of x. Which sum takes us from the root back to x?

ask.ifNot: A square root is the number that multiplies by itself to make x. So we go back the other way: x is 12 times 12, not 12 times 2.

beats.say: Here is why. Build a square with 12 rows of 12 tiles. Its side is the square root, and the number of tiles in it is x.
12 times 12 is a big one, so we split it. 12 times 10 is 120, and 12 times 2 is 24.
120 plus 24 is 144. So x is 144. There is our hidden number!
Good mathematicians always check. Put 144 in place of x: its square root is 12, and 12 plus 9 is 21. It works.
Two moves, in order: undo the plus, then undo the root by squaring. Your turn next!
We want the square of 21. It gets its name from a shape, so let's start with the shape.
A 21 by 21 square is too big for our board, so here is a baby one: 3 rows of 3 tiles. 3 times 3 is 9 tiles, so the square of 3 is 9.
Our square is the same idea, only bigger: 21 rows, with 21 tiles in each row. So which sum gives the square of 21?

ask.ifNot: Think of the square: 21 rows, and 21 tiles in every row. That is 21 lots of 21, so 21 times 21.

beats.say: Careful with that little 2 up in the air. It never means times 2. It tells us to multiply the number by itself.
21 times 21 is not in our tables, so we break the second 21 into 20 and 1.
21 times 20 is 420. And 21 times 1 is 21. What do they make together?

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly. Add the ones first, then the tens, then the hundreds. 420 plus 21 comes to 441.

beats.say: 420 plus 21 is 441. So the square of 21 is 441.
A quick check, going backwards: the square root of 441 is 21, because 21 times 21 is 441.
Remember: the square of a number is that number times itself, like the tiles in a square.
Look at this one. The square root of x, plus 14, makes 28. Our job is to find x itself.
Think of the square root of x as one closed box. The box plus 14 makes 28. So what do we clear away first?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side again. The root of x has a plus 14 hanging on to it. That goes first, and the root sign waits until the end.

beats.say: Plus 14 is undone by minus 14. Whatever we do on the left, we do on the right as well.
Now the root of x stands alone. And 28 minus 14 gives us 14.
Now the trap. We have found the square root of x, and that is 14. We have not found x yet! What undoes a square root?

ask.ifNot: A square root is the number that multiplies by itself to make x. So we go back the other way: x is 14 times 14, not 14 times 2.

beats.say: Think of a big square of tiles, 14 along each side. The side is the root, and all the tiles together are x. So x is 14 times 14.
14 times 14 is a big one, so we split it. 14 times 10 is 140, and 14 times 4 is 56.
140 plus 56 is 196. So x is 196. There is our hidden number!
Let's check it. The square root of 196 is 14, and 14 plus 14 is 28. It fits perfectly.
So the plan for a puzzle like this: first get the root on its own, then square it to find x.
Find the square root of 25. First, let's be sure what that is asking.
Which of these is the square root asking for?

ask.ifNot: A square root is not a half. It asks: which number, multiplied by itself, makes 25?

beats.say: Yes. The same number goes in both boxes: something times itself makes 25. Think of 25 tiles laid out as a perfect square. How long is one side?
Let's test some numbers. 4 times 4 is 16. That is too small.
Too small, so we go one bigger. What is 5 times 5?

ask.ifNot: 5 times 5 means 5 lots of 5. Count up in lots of 5 and you land on 25.

beats.say: 5 times 5 is exactly 25. Look: 25 tiles make a square with 5 on each side.
So the square root of 25 is 5.
So for a square root, hunt for the number that multiplies by itself to make it. Your times tables do the rest.
Look at this one. The square root of x, plus 2, makes 10. Our job is to find x itself.
The root of x is not alone on the left. Something is sitting next to it. What should we move out of the way first?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side again. The root of x has a plus 2 hanging on to it. That goes first, and the root sign waits until the end.

beats.say: Plus 2 is undone by minus 2. Whatever we do on the left, we do on the right as well.
On the left, only the root of x is left. On the right, 10 minus 2 is 8.
Now the trap. We have found the square root of x, and that is 8. We have not found x yet! What undoes a square root?

ask.ifNot: A square root is the number that multiplies by itself to make x. So we go back the other way: x is 8 times 8, not 8 times 2.

beats.say: Here is why. Build a square with 8 rows of 8 tiles. Its side is the square root, and the number of tiles in it is x.
8 times 8 is 64. So x is 64. There is our hidden number!
Good mathematicians always check. Put 64 in place of x: its square root is 8, and 8 plus 2 is 10. It works.
Two moves, in order: undo the plus, then undo the root by squaring. Your turn next!
We want the square of 12. It gets its name from a shape, so let's start with the shape.
Here is a square made of tiles. It has 12 rows, and 12 tiles in every row. The square of 12 is the number of tiles in it.
So which sum gives us the square of 12?

ask.ifNot: Look at the tiles. There are 12 rows, and each row has 12 tiles. That is 12 lots of 12, so 12 times 12.

beats.say: Careful with that little 2 up in the air. It never means times 2. It tells us to multiply the number by itself.
12 times 12 is not in our tables, so we break the second 12 into 10 and 2.
12 times 10 is 120. And 12 times 2 is 24. What do they make together?

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly. Add the ones first, then the tens, then the hundreds. 120 plus 24 comes to 144.

beats.say: 120 plus 24 is 144. So the square of 12 is 144.
A quick check, going backwards: the square root of 144 is 12, because 12 times 12 is 144.
So, to square a number, multiply it by itself. Never by 2!
We want the square root of 729. Before we hunt for it, what does a square root mean?
What is a square root question really asking?

ask.ifNot: A square root is not a half. It asks: which number, multiplied by itself, makes 729?

beats.say: So we need one number for both boxes. Picture 729 tiles arranged in a perfect square: the square root is the length of its side.
729 is too big for our tables, so we trap it between two squares we know. 20 times 20 is 400. 30 times 30 is 900.
729 sits between 400 and 900. So where is our number?

ask.ifNot: Look at the two lines. 729 is more than 400 and less than 900. So its root is more than 20 and less than 30.

beats.say: Now the clever clue: the last digit. 729 ends in 9. 3 times 3 is 9, and 7 times 7 is 49: both end in 9.
So our number ends in 3 or 7: it is 23 or 27. Now, 729 is closer to 900 than to 400. Which one shall we try?

ask.ifNot: 900 is the square of 30, and 729 is close to it. So we want the one nearer to 30, and that is 27.

beats.say: Let's test 27. Break the second 27 into 20 and 7. 27 times 20 is 540, and 27 times 7 is 189.
540 plus 189 is 729. That is our number exactly!
So the square root of 729 is 27.
That is the plan every time: squeeze it between two tens, read the last digit, and test your best guess by multiplying.
Find the square root of 100. First, let's be sure what that is asking.
Which of these is the square root asking for?

ask.ifNot: A square root is not a half. It asks: which number, multiplied by itself, makes 100?

beats.say: Yes. The same number goes in both boxes: something times itself makes 100. Think of 100 tiles laid out as a perfect square. How long is one side?
Let's test some numbers. 9 times 9 is 81. That is too small.
Too small, so we go one bigger. What is 10 times 10?

ask.ifNot: 10 times 10 means 10 lots of 10. Count up in lots of 10 and you land on 100.

beats.say: 10 times 10 is exactly 100. Look: 100 tiles make a square with 10 on each side.
So the square root of 100 is 10.
Remember: a square root is the side of the square. Find the number that, times itself, gives what you started with.
Look at this one. The square root of x, plus 7, makes 13. Our job is to find x itself.
Before we touch the root sign, we want the root of x standing by itself. What is in its way?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side again. The root of x has a plus 7 hanging on to it. That goes first, and the root sign waits until the end.

beats.say: So we subtract 7. Both sides, remember, or the balance tips.
On the left, only the root of x is left. On the right, 13 minus 7 is 6.
Don't put your pencil down yet. 6 is only the root of x. Which sum takes us from the root back to x?

ask.ifNot: A square root is the number that multiplies by itself to make x. So we go back the other way: x is 6 times 6, not 6 times 2.

beats.say: Here is why. Build a square with 6 rows of 6 tiles. Its side is the square root, and the number of tiles in it is x.
From our tables, 6 times 6 is 36. So x equals 36.
Let's check it. The square root of 36 is 6, and 6 plus 7 is 13. It fits perfectly.
So the plan for a puzzle like this: first get the root on its own, then square it to find x.
We want the square of 13. It gets its name from a shape, so let's start with the shape.
A 13 by 13 square is too big for our board, so here is a baby one: 3 rows of 3 tiles. 3 times 3 is 9 tiles, so the square of 3 is 9.
Our square is the same idea, only bigger: 13 rows, with 13 tiles in each row. So which sum gives the square of 13?

ask.ifNot: Think of the square: 13 rows, and 13 tiles in every row. That is 13 lots of 13, so 13 times 13.

beats.say: Careful with that little 2 up in the air. It never means times 2. It tells us to multiply the number by itself.
13 times 13 is not in our tables, so we break the second 13 into 10 and 3.
13 times 10 is 130. And 13 times 3 is 39. What do they make together?

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly. Add the ones first, then the tens, then the hundreds. 130 plus 39 comes to 169.

beats.say: 130 plus 39 is 169. So the square of 13 is 169.
And if we go backwards, the square root of 169 brings us home to 13. Square and square root undo each other.
So, to square a number, multiply it by itself. Never by 2!
Here is our puzzle. The square root of x, plus 12, equals 16. We are hunting for x, the number hiding under the root sign.
Before we touch the root sign, we want the root of x standing by itself. What is in its way?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side again. The root of x has a plus 12 hanging on to it. That goes first, and the root sign waits until the end.

beats.say: So we subtract 12. Both sides, remember, or the balance tips.
On the left, only the root of x is left. On the right, 16 minus 12 is 4.
Don't put your pencil down yet. 4 is only the root of x. Which sum takes us from the root back to x?

ask.ifNot: A square root is the number that multiplies by itself to make x. So we go back the other way: x is 4 times 4, not 4 times 2.

beats.say: Here is why. Build a square with 4 rows of 4 tiles. Its side is the square root, and the number of tiles in it is x.
4 times 4 is 16. So x is 16. There is our hidden number!
Good mathematicians always check. Put 16 in place of x: its square root is 4, and 4 plus 12 is 16. It works.
Two moves, in order: undo the plus, then undo the root by squaring. Your turn next!
Rohan buys 5 crayons at 10 rupees each, and hands over 70 rupees. We want the change that comes back.

board.text: 5 crayons at Rs.10 each. Pays Rs.70.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 70 rupees pays for the crayons, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the crayons
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 5 crayons, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 5 crayons at 10 rupees each: that is 5 times 10. 5 times 10 is 50.
Careful: 50 is only the cost, not the answer. Rohan paid 70. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 50 away from 70.

beats.say: From 70, take off the 50. That leaves 20.
So Rohan gets 20 rupees back.
A quick check. Cost plus change should give back the money paid: 50 plus 20 is 70. It works.
So a change sum takes two moves. First find the total cost. Then take it away from the money paid. Your turn next!
Priya pays 200 rupees for a bag. That is the cost price. It is sold at a profit of 15 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Picture two bars, one under the other. The cost price, 200 rupees, is on top. The selling price is below, with a question mark for now.
With a profit, the selling price is bigger than the cost price. So the bottom bar sticks out, and the bit that sticks out is the profit.
The profit is 15 per cent. But 15 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 200 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the classic trap. Profit per cent is always worked out on the cost price, never on the selling price. And per cent means out of every 100.
10 per cent is the easy one: it is one tenth. 200 divided by 10 is 20.
5 per cent is half of 10 per cent. Half of 20 is 10.
15 per cent is 10 per cent and 5 per cent together. 20 plus 10 makes 30. That is the profit.
So the profit is 30 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 200 plus 30 is 230. So the selling price is 230 rupees.
Does that make sense? A profit should lift the selling price above the cost price, and 230 is 30 more than 200. It fits.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. You can do the next one yourself!
Aarav pays 800 rupees for a tablet. That is the cost price. It is sold at a loss of 15 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Picture two bars, one under the other. The cost price, 800 rupees, is on top. The selling price is below, with a question mark for now.
With a loss, the selling price is smaller than the cost price. So the bottom bar stops short, and the gap is the loss.
The loss is 15 per cent. But 15 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 800 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Loss per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
First find 10 per cent. That is one tenth, so divide by 10. 800 divided by 10 gives 80.
5 per cent is half of 10 per cent. Half of 80 is 40.
15 per cent is 10 per cent and 5 per cent together. 80 plus 40 makes 120. That is the loss.
So the loss is 120 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 800 take away 120 is 680. So the selling price is 680 rupees.
Quick check. With a loss, the selling price must be smaller than the cost price. 680 is 120 below 800. Good.
So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. Your turn next!
Here we know the price of the whole lot: 10 stickers for 30 rupees. Our job is to find the price of one sticker.
Think of the 30 rupees as a bar shared into 10 equal pieces. Each piece is the price of one sticker.
So which sum finds the cost of one sticker?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 30 rupees equally among 10 stickers. Sharing equally is dividing.

beats.say: Think of the 10 times table. 10 times what makes 30? 10 times 3 is 30.
There it is: each sticker costs 3 rupees.
Check by building it back up. 10 stickers at 3 rupees each: 10 times 3 is 30. It fits.
Cost of many, and you want the cost of one? Divide the total cost by the number of things. You can do the next one yourself!
Here are 2 bags of sugar. Every bag weighs 10 kilograms 250 grams, and Siddharth wants the total weight in grams.

board.text: 2 bags of sugar, each 10 kg 250 g

spec.note: Each bag weighs 10 kg 250 g

beats.say: Look at how one bag is written: kilograms and grams mixed together. The answer must be in grams, so we change the kilograms. How many grams make 1 kilogram?

ask.ifNot: Kilo means a thousand. So 1 kilogram is 1000 grams.

beats.say: Grams are tiny next to kilograms, so the number has to grow: we multiply by 1000. 10 kilograms is 10 times 1000, which is 10000 grams.
Do not lose the 250 grams that came with it. 10000 plus 250 is 10250 grams, so now one bag is written in a single unit.

spec.note: Each bag weighs 10 kg 250 g

beats.say: Every bag weighs 10250 grams, and there are 2 of them. What shall we work out?

ask.ifNot: There are 2 bags, and each one is the full 10250 grams. So we need 2 lots of 10250: a multiplication.

beats.say: Doubling is easiest in two pieces. Double 10000 is 20000, and double 250 is 500.
Add the two pieces: 20000 plus 500 is 20500. So the 2 bags together weigh 20500 grams.
Does that make sense? The kilograms alone gave 20000 grams, and our answer is a little more, because every bag has 250 extra grams. Forgetting those extra grams is the slip to watch for.
So the plan for mixed units: first write one bag in a single unit, here grams. Then multiply by the number of bags.
We have a tank with 10 litres of water in it, and glasses that hold 300 millilitres each. Let's find how many glasses it fills.
Look at the units first. The tank is in litres, the glass is in millilitres, and those two do not mix. Which shall we change?

ask.ifNot: We can only compare amounts that are in the same unit. Changing the litres into millilitres keeps every number whole, so that is the friendly choice.

beats.say: Each litre is 1000 millilitres. Smaller unit, so more of them: we multiply by 1000. 10 times 1000 gives 10000 millilitres in the tank.
Now both are in millilitres, so we want to know how many lots of 300 fit into 10000. Take two zeros off each to make it friendlier: how many lots of 3 fit into 100?
3 does not go into 100 exactly. 3 times 33 is 99, and that is as close as we can get without going over.
So 33 glasses use 9900 millilitres. Take that from 10000, and 100 millilitres are left over.
Here is the bit to think about. There are 100 millilitres left in the tank. Can we count one more glass?

ask.ifNot: A glass only counts when it is full, and a full one needs 300 millilitres. We have just 100 left, so that last bit stays in the tank.

beats.say: The leftover 100 millilitres is not enough for another glass. So 33 glasses can be filled.
Let's be sure. Glass number 34 would bring the total to 10200 millilitres, and that is more than the 10000 the tank holds. So 33 is right.
So the plan: same units first, then divide. And when something is left over, ask what the leftover means before you round.
Here is a square, and each side is 9 centimetres. We want its area.
Area is the space inside the shape: how many little squares would cover it. Which rule gives us that for a square?

ask.ifNot: 4 times the side is the walk around the edge, and that is the perimeter. For the space inside we count rows of little squares: side times side.

beats.say: In a square every side is the same. So each row holds 9 little squares, and there are 9 rows as well. That is 9 times 9.
9 times 9 is 81. That is a tables fact worth knowing by heart.
So the area is 81 square centimetres. Careful: 9 times 9 means 9 rows of 9. It is not the same as doubling 9.
Check by undoing it. 81 shared into 9 rows gives 9 in each row. That is our side again.
So for the area of a square, multiply the side by itself. 4 times the side is a different question, the perimeter.
1100 centimetres. Same length, new unit: we want it in metres.
Start with the fact that links the two units. 1 metre is 100 centimetres. Think of a metre stick: it has 100 centimetres marked along it.
A metre is bigger than a centimetre. So will the number of metres be bigger or smaller than 1100?

ask.ifNot: It takes 100 centimetres to make just 1 metre. A bigger unit means fewer of them, so the number goes down: we divide.

beats.say: Every 100 centimetres make 1 metre, so we count how many lots of 100 are in 1100. 1100 divided by 100 is 11.
So 1100 centimetres is the same length as 11 metres.
Check by going back the other way. 11 metres, times 100, is 1100 centimetres. Just what we started with.
Remember the idea, not just the rule. Bigger units mean fewer of them, so going up to a bigger unit we divide.
3 bags of wheat, each one 6 kilograms 250 grams. Our job is to find what they weigh altogether, in grams.

board.text: 3 bags of wheat, each 6 kg 250 g

spec.note: Each bag weighs 6 kg 250 g

beats.say: One bag is written in two units at once, kilograms and grams, and those do not mix. We want grams, so let's turn the kilograms into grams. How many grams are in 1 kilogram?

ask.ifNot: Kilo means a thousand. So 1 kilogram is 1000 grams.

beats.say: 1 kilogram is 1000 grams. A gram is much smaller than a kilogram, so we need many more of them: that is why we multiply. 6 times 1000 is 6000 grams.
Do not lose the 250 grams that came with it. 6000 plus 250 is 6250 grams, so now one bag is written in a single unit.

spec.note: Each bag weighs 6 kg 250 g

beats.say: Every bag weighs 6250 grams, and there are 3 of them. What shall we work out?

ask.ifNot: There are 3 bags, and each one is the full 6250 grams. So we need 3 lots of 6250: a multiplication.

A bucket holds 12 litres of water, and each glass takes 200 millilitres. How many glasses can we fill?

ask.ifNot: We can only compare amounts that are in the same unit. Changing the litres into millilitres keeps every number whole, so that is the friendly choice.

beats.say: 1 litre is 1000 millilitres. A millilitre is much smaller, so we need many more of them, and that means multiply. 12 times 1000 is 12000 millilitres.
Now both amounts are in millilitres. How do we find how many 200 millilitre glasses fit into 12000 millilitres?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing the water out into equal glasses. Finding how many equal groups fit is a division.

Check by pouring it back. 60 glasses of 200 millilitres is 60 times 200, which is 12000 millilitres. That is the whole bucket, with nothing left over.

Our rectangle is 18 centimetres long and 4 centimetres wide. The question asks for its area.

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides takes you along the edges, and that is the perimeter, the walk around. For the space inside we count rows of squares: length times width.

Check by undoing it. 72 shared into 4 rows gives 18 in each row, and that is our length. It fits.
Remember: area means the space inside, so multiply length by width. Adding the sides is for the walk around the edge.

board.text: 7 erasers at Rs.4 each. Pays Rs.38.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 38 rupees pays for the erasers, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the erasers
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 7 erasers, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 7 erasers at 4 rupees each: that is 7 times 4. 7 times 4 is 28.
Careful: 28 is only the cost, not the answer. Tara paid 38. So how do we find the change?
